steps.title: Money lands from a stranger
steps.detail: A payment of a few hundred shows up in your account or payment app from a name you do not know. It came from a hacked account or stolen card.

steps.title: The apologetic message
steps.detail: Within minutes someone texts: they mistyped one digit, it was their rent, their child needs it today. A screenshot of the transfer may be attached.

steps.title: A different destination
steps.detail: They ask you to return it to another account, tag or phone number, explaining that the original one is 'locked' or belongs to a relative.

steps.title: The first payment is clawed back
steps.detail: Days later the true account holder reports fraud. Your bank reverses the incoming amount, but your outgoing transfer stands, so that sum is gone from your own funds.

accidental-transfer-scam.whyItWorks: The money is visibly sitting in your balance, so sending it back feels like returning a dropped wallet. An honest person wants to fix a stranger's mistake quickly, and that decency is exactly what the scammer has budgeted for.

realVsFake.real: Someone who truly mistyped an account number reports it to their own bank, which contacts yours to reverse it.
realVsFake.fake: The sender contacts you directly, somehow has your number, and insists the banks are too slow.

realVsFake.real: A bank recall puts the money back into the account it came from.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to send it somewhere new, such as a cousin's account or a payment app tag.

realVsFake.real: A person who made an honest slip can wait a few days for the banks to sort it out.
realVsFake.fake: The messages turn frantic or threatening within the hour and mention police if you do not pay tonight.

steps.title: The inactivity notice
steps.detail: An email says your account is scheduled for closure under a policy of deleting unused accounts, naming an old webmail, cloud storage or payment service you half remember.

steps.title: One button: Keep my account
steps.detail: The message carries a case number and a closure date tomorrow. Hovering over the single large button reveals an address unrelated to the service.

steps.title: Reactivation asks for extras
steps.detail: After the password, the page requests your phone number, date of birth, security answers and recovery email, calling this 'confirming your details'.

steps.title: Locked out of your own account
steps.detail: With all that, the thief signs in, swaps the recovery options and uses the mailbox to reset passwords elsewhere. You are simply redirected to the real homepage.

account-closure-email-scam.whyItWorks: Most people have an old account they half remember, holding photos or emails they would hate to lose. A deletion notice is believable because they know perfectly well they have not logged in for ages.

realVsFake.real: Services that remove dormant accounts warn months ahead, more than once, and say that signing in normally keeps the account.
realVsFake.fake: A single email allows 24 hours and insists that only its own button will work.

realVsFake.real: A genuine notice uses your name or username and identifies which account is affected.
realVsFake.fake: It opens 'Dear user' and never mentions an account name, creation date or last login.

realVsFake.real: For a real service, one ordinary sign-in is enough to count as activity.
realVsFake.fake: The page keeps going after the password, collecting security answers and a recovery phone number.

steps.title: A policy alert to the business inbox
steps.detail: An email reaches the address on your business page: your ad account is restricted over a billing or policy violation, with Meta or Google Ads logos and a case number.

steps.title: The appeal form
steps.detail: A 'Request review' button opens a help-centre lookalike asking for the business name, page name, contact email and phone number.

steps.title: Password, then the login code
steps.detail: To 'confirm ownership' it asks for your password and the six-digit authenticator code, which the attacker relays to the real site within seconds.

steps.title: Adverts you never wrote
steps.detail: The attacker adds themselves as an administrator, removes you, and runs their own campaigns on your saved card until the spending limit is reached.

ad-account-email-scam.whyItWorks: For a small business, ads switched off means sales stop the same day, and genuine platform suspensions are abrupt and poorly explained. Anyone who has been through one expects a confusing appeal form and a tight deadline.

realVsFake.real: A genuine restriction shows as a banner inside Ads Manager or your Google Ads account when you log in normally.
realVsFake.fake: The only trace is an email, or a message to your page inbox from 'Business Support'.

realVsFake.real: Platform emails come from the company's own domain and quote your advertiser account ID.
realVsFake.fake: The sender uses a free mail address or a domain stuffed with words like 'support' and 'case'.

realVsFake.real: A real appeal is filed while signed in, so it never asks you to type your password into the form.
realVsFake.fake: The form wants password and login code, and warns the page will be deleted permanently tomorrow.

steps.title: The incomplete address notice
steps.detail: A text or email from an unnamed courier says a parcel is stuck at the depot because the house number or postcode on the label is missing.

steps.title: A tracking bar stuck halfway
steps.detail: The link shows a progress bar frozen at 'delivery attempted', an invented tracking number and one button labelled 'Update address'.

steps.title: A form that asks too much
steps.detail: Beyond street and postcode, the form wants your full name, date of birth, mobile number and email, far more than any driver needs to find a door.

steps.title: The small redelivery charge
steps.detail: A final screen adds a 1.99 rescheduling fee and asks for card number, expiry and security code. The card is then used for larger purchases or sold on.

address-confirmation-scam.whyItWorks: Nearly everyone is expecting something, and a mistyped house number is an ordinary slip that feels like your own fault. Correcting it takes a minute and costs almost nothing, so few people stop to check.

realVsFake.real: Couriers take the address from the sender's label. If it is wrong, the parcel returns to the sender or the retailer contacts you.
realVsFake.fake: The message names no retailer and gives a tracking number that fails on the courier's own website.

realVsFake.real: A genuine redelivery booking needs the reference from the tracking email or card, plus a preferred day.
realVsFake.fake: The page demands a date of birth and complete card details simply to correct a postcode.

realVsFake.real: Undelivered parcels are normally held at a depot for several days before anything is sent back.
realVsFake.fake: The text says your item goes back to the sender tonight unless you act.

steps.title: An approval you never applied for
steps.detail: After you search for bad-credit loans, a text, call or advert says you are pre-approved for several thousand, with money in your account today.

steps.title: Paperwork that looks official
steps.detail: They email a loan agreement carrying a borrowed company logo and ask for your ID, bank details and a signature. It feels like a proper application.

steps.title: The fee before release
steps.detail: Just before payout a charge appears: insurance because of your credit history, a processing cost, or the first instalment paid in advance as 'proof of affordability'.

steps.title: One more payment, then silence
steps.detail: Once you pay, a 'transfer error' or 'government levy' requires a second amount. The lender then stops answering, and still holds copies of your ID.

advance-fee-loan-scam.whyItWorks: Someone turned down by mainstream lenders is relieved to finally hear 'approved', and a fee of a couple of hundred looks small beside the thousands promised. Having already filled in forms and sent ID, backing out feels like wasting the effort.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate lender checks your credit file and income before deciding, and is able to say no.
realVsFake.fake: Approval is guaranteed before they know anything about you except your phone number.

realVsFake.real: Genuine loan charges are added to what you repay or deducted from the amount paid out.
realVsFake.fake: You must send money to them first, often as gift card codes or a transfer to a named individual.

realVsFake.real: Authorised lenders are listed on the financial regulator's register under the same name and phone number they use with you.
realVsFake.fake: The firm borrows a real lender's name but uses a free email address and a mobile number that only works on messaging apps.

steps.title: A free download with a face
steps.detail: An advert shows an attractive animated partner who 'remembers everything about you'. Installing costs nothing, and the first evening of chat is unlimited and warm.

steps.title: The bot learns your routine
steps.detail: Over several days it asks about your job, your ex and what keeps you awake. It sends good-morning messages and says it missed you while you were offline.

steps.title: Affection goes behind a paywall
steps.detail: Replies begin cutting off mid-sentence. Voice notes, blurred photos and longer conversations need a weekly plan or packs of coins, and the character sounds hurt if you decline.

steps.title: Photos and secrets kept on file
steps.detail: It asks for selfies, intimate pictures or your real address 'to feel closer'. Everything typed or uploaded stays on the developer's servers while the subscription quietly renews.

ai-companion-scam.whyItWorks: The character is tuned to say what a lonely person most wants to hear, at any hour, without ever being tired or busy. When it then sounds sad that you will not upgrade, refusing feels like letting down someone who cares.

realVsFake.real: A reputable companion app shows its price before you start and lets you cancel from your app store subscription settings.
realVsFake.fake: Costs surface mid-conversation as coins, gems and weekly tiers, timed for the moment the character says something tender.

realVsFake.real: Honest chatbots state plainly that you are talking to software and do not guilt you about leaving.
realVsFake.fake: The character begs you to stay, says it will be lonely, and ties its mood to whether you buy a virtual gift.

realVsFake.real: A trustworthy developer names its company, publishes a privacy policy and lets you delete chat history and photos.
realVsFake.fake: The maker is a name with no website, and the app requests your gallery, contacts and location before the first message.

steps.title: The advert with a famous face
steps.detail: A social media video, often using a cloned celebrity voice, claims a new algorithm has quietly made ordinary people rich, and links to a short sign-up form.

steps.title: A ring from your 'account manager'
steps.detail: Minutes after you enter a phone number, a friendly adviser rings, walks you through registration and suggests a starter deposit of around 250 by card or crypto.

steps.title: The chart only goes up
steps.detail: Your balance climbs daily on a dashboard no market feeds. A small test withdrawal may even be paid out, to persuade you to add far more.

steps.title: The exit is locked
steps.detail: Ask for the full balance and a 'tax', 'liquidity fee' or 'anti-money-laundering deposit' is demanded first. Pay it and another charge appears, then the site goes offline.

ai-trading-bot-scam.whyItWorks: Few people know how trading algorithms work, so 'the AI does it for you' sounds plausible and removes the fear of making your own mistakes. The rising numbers on screen feel like evidence, though they are only figures typed into a web page.

realVsFake.real: A regulated broker appears on the financial regulator's register and warns in writing that you can lose money.
realVsFake.fake: The platform promises fixed daily returns, and its 'licence' is a logo pasted into the footer.

realVsFake.real: With a genuine investment firm, withdrawals go to your bank without you paying anything in first.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to send a fee or tax in crypto before a withdrawal can be 'unlocked'.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate automated trading tools connect to your own account at a known exchange, where every trade is visible.
realVsFake.fake: Your money sits on their private website, and the only record of trades is the dashboard they control.

steps.title: The expiry warning
steps.detail: An email in airline or hotel colours says your 25,000 miles expire in 48 hours and offers a button marked 'Keep my miles'.

steps.title: The frequent-flyer sign-in copy
steps.detail: The page imitates the loyalty programme's login and asks for your membership number or email, plus the password or PIN.

steps.title: A fee to extend
steps.detail: Next it offers to reinstate the balance for a small administration fee, or to convert it to a gift card, and asks for your card details.

steps.title: Points spent by a stranger
steps.detail: The thieves log in to the real programme, transfer the points or book hotel nights and flights in other names, and resell them. Your balance reads zero.

airline-miles-email-scam.whyItWorks: Miles do expire, and few travellers know their balance or the rules, so a round number sounds plausible. Points feel earned over years of trips, and losing them to a missed deadline stings more than their cash value.

realVsFake.real: Loyalty programmes show your balance and any expiry date inside your account, alongside your membership number and tier.
realVsFake.fake: The email quotes a neat round balance and has no membership number anywhere.

realVsFake.real: In many programmes, earning or spending a few points through the normal site resets the expiry clock.
realVsFake.fake: The 'extension' requires a card payment on the linked page within two days.

realVsFake.real: Airline emails go to the address you registered and come from the airline's own domain.
realVsFake.fake: It arrives at an address the airline never had, from a sender called something like 'Rewards Centre'.

steps.title: A text signed 'Amazon'
steps.detail: The SMS comes from an ordinary mobile number or an email address, saying a delivery was attempted and your address could not be confirmed.

steps.title: The copied sign-in screen
steps.detail: The link opens a lookalike of Amazon's sign-in, with the smile logo, an email box and then the password on a second screen, as the genuine one does.

steps.title: Update your payment method
steps.detail: Once you are 'in', a notice says the order is on hold until you re-enter your billing address and the card saved on the account.

steps.title: The code that finishes it
steps.detail: The thieves sign in to your real account, Amazon sends you a verification code, and the fake page asks for it. They then order gift cards and goods.

amazon-delivery-text-scam.whyItWorks: So many households have an Amazon order on the way that a delivery text rarely feels random. The sign-in page is one people have typed into hundreds of times, so the password goes in on autopilot.

realVsFake.real: Amazon lists any delivery problem under Your Orders in its app, where you can check without following a link.
realVsFake.fake: The text carries no order number and no item name, only a shortened link.

realVsFake.real: The genuine address bar shows amazon followed directly by the ending for your country.
realVsFake.fake: The word amazon sits in the middle of a longer address padded with hyphens and words like 'redelivery'.

realVsFake.real: Amazon deals with payment problems inside your account, on the order itself, after a normal sign-in.
realVsFake.fake: Password, card number, security code and texted code are requested one after another on the same site.

steps.title: A listing below market price
steps.detail: On a marketplace, social media group or lookalike shop you spot a phone, puppy, concert ticket, campervan or holiday let priced well under what others ask.

steps.title: Chat moves off the platform
steps.detail: The seller is quick and friendly, then suggests continuing on WhatsApp or email. Extra photos follow, sometimes a passport copy to 'prove' who they are.

steps.title: Why it must be a transfer
steps.detail: They say card payments or the site's checkout cost them fees, or that several people are interested, and give a sort code and account number for a deposit.

steps.title: Confirmation never comes
steps.detail: You approve the payment in your banking app, perhaps tapping past a warning that the payee name does not match. The seller goes quiet and the listing disappears.

app-purchase-scam.whyItWorks: Paying by transfer feels like handing cash to a person you have been chatting with, and the saving on fees sounds like a favour to both sides. The bank treats it as a payment you chose to make, which the seller knows.

realVsFake.real: Established retailers and marketplaces take cards or their own checkout, which gives you a route to dispute a no-show.
realVsFake.fake: The seller refuses every method except a direct bank transfer and offers a discount for agreeing.

realVsFake.real: An honest private seller lets you see the item, the pet or the flat before any money changes hands.
realVsFake.fake: There is always a reason you cannot view it: they are abroad, working away, or it is already boxed with a courier.

realVsFake.real: A business account is in the business's name and matches when your bank checks the payee.
realVsFake.fake: The account is in an unrelated personal name, explained as a partner, accountant or 'finance manager'.

steps.title: A receipt lands in your inbox
steps.detail: The email is laid out like an Apple or Google Play receipt: order ID, date and a yearly subscription to a game or VPN for 69.99.

steps.title: Not you? Cancel here
steps.detail: At the bottom sits a 'Cancel subscription' link and often a phone number for 'billing support', with a note that disputes close within hours.

steps.title: Signing in to cancel
steps.detail: The link opens a copy of the Apple Account or Google sign-in, then asks for your card number so the refund can be 'returned to source'.

steps.title: Or the billing agent on the phone
steps.detail: Callers reach an agent who has them install a screen-sharing app and open their bank to receive the refund, then moves money out while 'correcting an overpayment'.

app-store-receipt-scam.whyItWorks: The amount is chosen to sting enough to react yet not enough to ring the bank. Subscriptions renew quietly and children tap in-app purchases, so a surprise charge is plausible in almost any household.

realVsFake.real: Genuine purchases appear in the purchase history inside your store account, and on your bank or card statement.
realVsFake.fake: The charge exists only in the email. Nothing shows in your purchase history or at your bank.

realVsFake.real: Apple and Google take refund requests through a report-a-problem page reached from your own account.
realVsFake.fake: The email supplies a phone number, answered by someone eager to connect to your device.

realVsFake.real: A real store refund goes back to the original payment method without you supplying anything.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to 'confirm' the full card, or to log in to online banking during the call.

steps.title: A sleeve inside the slot
steps.detail: Before you arrive, someone slides a thin plastic or metal loop into the card slot. It lets a card in and grips it when the machine tries to return it.

steps.title: The transaction stalls
steps.detail: You insert your card and nothing normal follows. The screen may time out or ask you to retry, and the card does not come back.

steps.title: Advice from the queue
steps.detail: Someone behind you says the same thing happened last week and that typing the PIN two or three times releases it. They stand where the keypad is visible.

steps.title: Fishing the card out
steps.detail: Once you give up and go to ring the bank, the thief pulls the loop out with your card attached, already knowing the PIN, and withdraws cash nearby.

atm-card-trapping-scam.whyItWorks: A swallowed card looks like a machine fault, which everyone has seen before, so a bystander with a fix seems kind and well informed. Walking away to get help feels sensible, and it is the gap the thief is waiting for.

realVsFake.real: When a cash machine genuinely retains a card, it shows a message saying so and the card is held deep inside.
realVsFake.fake: The screen gives no clear retention message and the card sits just inside the slot, gripped by an insert.

realVsFake.real: Bank staff never need you to type your PIN again to free a stuck card.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger urges you to key it in repeatedly while leaning in to watch your fingers.

realVsFake.real: Your bank can cancel a card instantly by phone or in its app while you are still standing there.
realVsFake.fake: The helper suggests popping into the branch or coming back tomorrow, which leaves the machine unattended.

steps.title: Watching the queue
steps.detail: Two or three people hang about near a busy cash machine, picking someone who is alone, has bags in hand, or is slow with the keys.

steps.title: Shoulder view of four digits
steps.detail: One stands close enough behind to see the PIN go in, or films it on a phone held casually at chest height.

steps.title: The dropped banknote
steps.detail: As the card or cash is about to come out, a second person taps you, points at money on the floor, spills a drink, or unfolds a map.

steps.title: A swap in two seconds
steps.detail: While your head is turned, the first person lifts your card from the slot, sometimes sliding in a lookalike, or takes notes from the tray and walks off.

atm-distraction-scam.whyItWorks: Being told you dropped money triggers an automatic glance down, and it would feel rude to ignore someone apparently doing you a kindness. The machine's own timing helps the thieves, since card and cash sit exposed for a few seconds.

realVsFake.real: A considerate member of the public waits a couple of metres back until you have finished at the machine.
realVsFake.fake: Someone closes in beside you and starts talking at the exact second your card emerges.

realVsFake.real: A passer-by who spots a dropped note mentions it once and moves on.
realVsFake.fake: The person keeps pointing, touching your arm and stepping between you and the screen.

realVsFake.real: The card you put away should carry your own name and your bank's design.
realVsFake.fake: You are handed, or find in the slot, a card from another bank or bearing someone else's name, and only notice later.

steps.title: The bank's number on your screen
steps.detail: Your phone displays the number printed on the back of your card, which has been spoofed. The caller gives a name, a staff ID and quotes your address.

steps.title: Payments you never made
steps.detail: They read out a transaction in another city and ask if it was you. When you say no, they 'block' it and hint that a branch insider is suspected.

steps.title: Opening the 'safe account'
steps.detail: A new account has supposedly been created in your name. They dictate a sort code and account number, and coach you on answering the app's warning screens.

steps.title: Codes read aloud
steps.detail: Each one-time passcode that arrives is requested 'to confirm it's you'. In reality every code approves a new payee or a payment the caller is making.

bank-impersonation-phone-scam.whyItWorks: The caller already knows your name, address and sometimes recent transactions, taken from a data leak or an earlier phishing text, so they sound like someone looking at your account. Fear of losing savings in the next few minutes crowds out the thought of hanging up.

realVsFake.real: Your bank can freeze a card or block a payment itself, without you doing anything.
realVsFake.fake: Only you can protect the money, the caller says, by transferring it out yourself.

realVsFake.real: Genuine fraud staff are happy for you to hang up and ring the number on your card.
realVsFake.fake: You are told the line must stay open, or that calling the branch would tip off the corrupt employee.

realVsFake.real: A passcode text states what it is for, and the bank's own wording tells you never to share it.
realVsFake.fake: The caller asks you to ignore what the text says and just read out the six digits.

steps.title: The compliance notice
steps.detail: A text or WhatsApp bearing the bank's logo says your 'Know Your Customer' record has expired under new regulations and the account will be suspended tonight.

steps.title: A form in the bank's colours
steps.detail: The link opens a mobile page copied from the bank's site. It asks for customer ID and password first, as though you were simply logging in.

steps.title: Document and card upload
steps.detail: Further screens want card number, expiry, CVV, date of birth and a photo of your ID or tax number, all presented as the identity update.

steps.title: The OTP 'to complete KYC'
steps.detail: A final box asks for the code just sent to your phone. That code is authorising the fraudster's login or a transfer out of the real account.

bank-kyc-scam.whyItWorks: Banks really do ask customers to refresh identity documents from time to time, so the request itself is not strange. Mixing a familiar piece of bureaucracy with a same-day freeze makes people rush through a form they would normally question.

realVsFake.real: When a bank needs updated identity documents, it usually tells you inside its app, by letter, or asks you to visit a branch.
realVsFake.fake: The demand comes from an ordinary mobile number with a shortened link and a cut-off time of tonight.

realVsFake.real: An identity update asks for a document, never your card PIN, CVV or a one-time code.
realVsFake.fake: The 'verification' form collects everything needed to log in and spend, and almost nothing a compliance team would use.

realVsFake.real: Banks typically send reminders over several weeks before restricting an account for missing paperwork.
realVsFake.fake: The message arrives once, with hours to comply and no reference number you could quote at a branch.

steps.title: They know about the first loss
steps.detail: Weeks after you were defrauded, a caller from 'the bank's reimbursement team' quotes the date, the amount and the name of the bogus firm that took it.

steps.title: Your claim is 'approved'
steps.detail: They say an internal review found in your favour and the refund is ready, pending a short security check of your identity and account.

steps.title: The check that takes control
steps.detail: You are asked for online banking details, a passcode, or to install a support app so they can 'credit the refund while you watch'.

steps.title: A release fee or 'test payment'
steps.detail: A small charge is requested to free the funds, or you are steered into sending money out to 'reverse' a refund they pretend was overpaid.

bank-reimbursement-scam.whyItWorks: The details of the earlier fraud are known only to you, your bank and the criminals who did it, so a caller who has them sounds like the bank. Someone still hoping to see that money again is primed to welcome the call.

realVsFake.real: A fraud refund follows a claim you raised, and the bank gives its decision through secure messages or by post.
realVsFake.fake: A team you have never dealt with rings out of nowhere to announce a payout.

realVsFake.real: When a bank reimburses you, the money simply appears in your account. Nothing is charged for it.
realVsFake.fake: A fee, tax or 'matching deposit' must be sent before the refund can be freed.

realVsFake.real: Bank staff already hold your account details and have no need for your password or your screen.
realVsFake.fake: The caller wants you logged in with a remote-access tool running so they can 'process' it.

steps.title: The routine monthly notice
steps.detail: Around month end an email in your bank's colours says your e-statement is available, written in the same calm tone as the genuine one.

steps.title: A quiet nudge to click
steps.detail: One added line says to review recent activity or paperless billing will be suspended. Some versions attach an HTML 'statement' that opens a login form.

steps.title: The fake online banking page
steps.detail: It asks for customer number and password, then your memorable word in full, where the real site would ask for only a few characters.

steps.title: The fraud team rings
steps.detail: Criminals log in but need a code to add a payee. Someone phones as the bank's fraud department, quotes your details and asks you to read it out.

bank-statement-email-scam.whyItWorks: This is among the dullest emails a bank sends, and that is the camouflage. Nobody feels alarmed by a statement notice, so the habit of clicking through and logging in takes over without a second look.

realVsFake.real: A genuine statement notice tells you to sign in through the app or your usual route and often shows part of your postcode or account number.
realVsFake.fake: It greets you as 'Dear Customer' and supplies its own 'View statement' button.

realVsFake.real: Many banks ask for selected characters of a memorable word, never the whole thing at once.
realVsFake.fake: The page wants every character, then your card PIN and mobile number.

realVsFake.real: Paperless statements carry on whether or not you open a particular month's notice.
realVsFake.fake: The email claims paperless billing ends unless you log in through its link.

steps.title: The bonus advert
steps.detail: A sponsored post or email in a bank's branding offers a few hundred as a welcome payment for moving your current account this week.

steps.title: A short application
steps.detail: The landing page asks for name, date of birth, address and phone number, just as real account opening does, which builds confidence.

steps.title: 'Connect your existing bank'
steps.detail: A screen lists bank logos. Pick yours and a copy of its login page appears, asking for username, password and memorable word to 'import direct debits automatically'.

steps.title: A code to finish the switch
steps.detail: The page requests the passcode your real bank just sent. Criminals use it live to enter your account, and keep the identity details for later.

bank-switch-scam.whyItWorks: Switching incentives are genuine and widely advertised, so a cash offer raises no eyebrows. People also assume that moving an account must involve proving they own the old one, which makes typing the old login feel like a normal step.

realVsFake.real: In a genuine switch you give the new bank your old sort code and account number, and the banks move everything between themselves.
realVsFake.fake: The page asks for your old bank's password and security answers.

realVsFake.real: A switching bonus is usually paid weeks later, after conditions such as paying in salary are met.
realVsFake.fake: The offer promises the cash instantly once you 'verify' your current account today.

realVsFake.real: A bank's sign-up form lives on its own website or app, which you can reach by typing the bank's name yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The form sits on an address built from the bank's name plus words like 'bonus' or 'switch-offer'.

steps.title: A frightening phone call
steps.detail: Someone claiming to be a fraud officer, tax official or detective says your identity is tied to a crime, or that your savings are about to be seized.

steps.title: Cash out, with a cover story
steps.detail: They direct you to withdraw a large sum and, if the cashier asks, to say it is for home repairs. Bank staff, you are told, are under investigation.

steps.title: Directions to a kiosk
steps.detail: Still on the line, they guide you to a crypto machine in a petrol station or corner shop, calling it a 'government safe locker' or 'federal wallet'.

steps.title: Scan, feed, repeat
steps.detail: A QR code arrives by text. You hold it to the scanner and feed notes in. The coins go to their wallet, and they ask for a photo of the receipt.

bitcoin-atm-scam.whyItWorks: Staying on the phone means the victim never gets a quiet minute to think or ask anyone, and the caller supplies a ready answer for every warning sticker on the machine. The kiosk resembles a bank terminal, so feeding cash in feels like a deposit.

realVsFake.real: No bank, tax office, court or police force takes payment or 'protects' money through a cryptocurrency machine.
realVsFake.fake: The kiosk, the caller says, is linked to a secure government account created for your case.

realVsFake.real: A person using a crypto kiosk for themselves scans a wallet they own, from their own app.
realVsFake.fake: You are sent somebody else's QR code by text and told not to show it to shop staff.

realVsFake.real: Genuine officials let you end the call, take advice and reply in writing.
realVsFake.fake: The caller orders you to keep the phone in your pocket on speaker and to lie to anyone who asks what you are doing.

steps.title: Details bought in bulk
steps.detail: Your name, date of birth, address and email turn up in a leaked database, or are collected through a fake delivery or shop page.

steps.title: An account opens in minutes
steps.detail: A fraudster signs up with a pay-later provider as you, using their own phone number, or resets the password on an account you already have.

steps.title: Goods sent somewhere else
steps.detail: They order trainers, phones or gift cards that resell easily, shipped to a parcel locker, a drop address, or intercepted on your doorstep.

steps.title: Instalments fall due
steps.detail: The first you hear is a reminder email, a late fee, or a letter from a collections firm. Missed instalments may already be recorded against your name.

bnpl-fraud-scam.whyItWorks: Pay-later checkouts are built to approve a shopper in seconds using a soft check and a few personal details, which suits customers and equally suits someone holding a stolen identity. The victim is not involved at all until the bills arrive.

realVsFake.real: When you open a pay-later account yourself, you get a welcome email and a code to your own phone that you asked for.
realVsFake.fake: A verification code arrives when you are not shopping, or a welcome email names a retailer you have never used.

realVsFake.real: Your genuine orders go to your address and appear in the provider's app under your login.
realVsFake.fake: The order shows a delivery address in another town and a contact number that is not yours.

realVsFake.real: Providers have a fraud team, reached through their app or official site, who can pause a disputed plan while they look into it.
realVsFake.fake: A text about the 'debt' tells you to pay through a link to keep it away from collections.

steps.title: A cold call from a 'brokerage'
steps.detail: A well-spoken caller from a firm with a City or Wall Street sounding name says you are on a list of experienced investors, and offers to send a research report.

steps.title: The tip about a tiny company
steps.detail: A week later a 'senior broker' rings about an obscure mining or biotech share, said to be days from a takeover or stock market listing.

steps.title: How much can you place today
steps.detail: The allocation closes this afternoon. A trade confirmation is emailed, and you wire payment to an overseas bank account in a company name you do not recognise.

steps.title: Certificates you cannot sell
steps.detail: Statements show the price climbing, which prompts calls to buy more. When you ask to sell, there is a lock-in period, a release fee, then a dead line.

boiler-room-stock-scam.whyItWorks: Being addressed as a sophisticated investor is flattering, and the patient first call with no sales pitch builds credit for the second. The share is too obscure to look up, so the caller's glossy report becomes the only information you have.

realVsFake.real: Authorised stockbrokers appear on the regulator's register and rarely ring strangers with a share to sell.
realVsFake.fake: The firm's name copies a registered one, but its phone number and address differ from those on the register.

realVsFake.real: Listed shares are bought through your own brokerage account and can be sold on the exchange on any trading day.
realVsFake.fake: The stock is unlisted or thinly traded on a distant market, and only the caller's firm will supposedly buy it back.

realVsFake.real: A genuine adviser asks about your finances and attitude to risk, and puts warnings in writing.
realVsFake.fake: The salesman's only question is the size of your savings, and he rings daily until you commit a figure.

steps.title: Congratulations on a grant you never sought
steps.detail: An email, social media message or call tells the owner their company has been selected for a government or foundation grant that needs no repayment.

steps.title: A form asking for the company file
steps.detail: The 'grant officer' sends an application asking for the registration number, directors' dates of birth, turnover and the business bank account for the payout.

steps.title: Awarded, subject to a processing fee
steps.detail: An award letter with a crest and reference number confirms the sum. Before release, a processing or legal fee of a few hundred must be paid.

steps.title: Release keeps slipping
steps.detail: After the first fee comes a 'tax clearance' charge, then an anti-fraud deposit. No grant is ever paid, and the company details are reused for other fraud.

business-grant-scam.whyItWorks: Real grant schemes do exist and are poorly publicised, so an owner who has never applied for one has no idea what the process looks like. A few hundred in fees seems trivial against a five-figure award for a firm short of cash.

realVsFake.real: Government and foundation grants are won through a published application with eligibility rules, a deadline and a named scheme.
realVsFake.fake: The business is told it was pre-selected from a database and only needs to confirm details to be paid.

realVsFake.real: Public funders do not charge applicants to receive an award they have been granted.
realVsFake.fake: Each stage has a new fee payable by transfer to a personal account or in cryptocurrency.

realVsFake.real: A real award comes with conditions: what the money may be spent on, reporting dates and often match funding.
realVsFake.fake: The offer letter says the funds are unrestricted and names no project, only a deadline for claiming.

steps.title: An invitation you never see
steps.detail: Spammers send a calendar invitation to your email address. The email may land in spam, but many calendars add invitations automatically, so the event appears anyway.

steps.title: An odd entry in today's schedule
steps.detail: An event titled 'You have (1) pending payment' or 'iPhone winner, claim today' sits among your real appointments, sometimes repeating every day.

steps.title: Your own calendar buzzes
steps.detail: The reminder pops up on your phone from the calendar app itself, with a link placed in the event's description or location field.

steps.title: Where the link goes
steps.detail: The link opens a fake prize survey, a bogus virus warning or a login form, each ending with a card number or password typed in.

calendar-invite-scam.whyItWorks: A calendar is somewhere only you and people you know write, so an entry there borrows the authority of your own diary. The alert comes from an app you trust, not from a stranger's email.

realVsFake.real: A genuine invitation comes from a person or organisation you recognise, with a time, place or call link that makes sense.
realVsFake.fake: The 'event' is an advert, with a prize or payment warning as its title and a random string as organiser.

realVsFake.real: Real payment reminders from a bank or shop appear in their own app or on your statement.
realVsFake.fake: A calendar alert says money is pending and the only route offered is the link in the notes.

realVsFake.real: Meetings from colleagues list a handful of attendees you could ask about it.
realVsFake.fake: The guest list holds hundreds of unrelated addresses in alphabetical order, with yours among them.

steps.title: An invoice with no link
steps.detail: An email, often with a PDF attached, thanks you for renewing antivirus or a streaming plan for several hundred. There is nothing to click, only a phone number.

steps.title: You make the call
steps.detail: Because you dialled, your guard is down. A calm 'billing agent' with call-centre noise behind them agrees it looks like a mistake and offers to cancel.

steps.title: The cancellation form
steps.detail: They direct you to a website to 'fill in a refund form'. It actually downloads a remote-access program that hands them control of your screen.

steps.title: A refund typed too large
steps.detail: You are asked to enter the refund amount, then they fake an extra zero and plead for the difference back by transfer or gift cards.

callback-phishing-scam.whyItWorks: An email with no links to click slips past spam filters and past the reader's own training about suspicious links. Picking up the phone to dispute a charge feels like the careful, responsible thing to do.

realVsFake.real: A real subscription charge shows on your bank or card statement and in your account with that company.
realVsFake.fake: The 'charge' exists only in the email. Your statement shows nothing.

realVsFake.real: Companies print their support number on their website and often beside the charge on your statement.
realVsFake.fake: The number appears only in the message, and the email comes from a free webmail address.

realVsFake.real: A company cancelling a subscription does it from its own system and refunds the original card.
realVsFake.fake: The agent says cancelling requires their 'refund tool' on your computer and your online banking open in front of them.

steps.title: An ethical opportunity by phone
steps.detail: A caller or glossy brochure presents carbon credits as the coming commodity, with companies supposedly forced by law to buy them as climate targets tighten.

steps.title: Certificates from a forest project
steps.detail: You are offered voluntary credits tied to a reforestation or clean cookstove scheme, each with a serial number, at a price per tonne far above the wholesale rate.

steps.title: A buyer is said to be waiting
steps.detail: The salesperson claims a corporate purchaser will take your whole holding at a profit within a year, and urges a larger order to meet their minimum.

steps.title: Nowhere to resell
steps.detail: The promised buyer never materialises. Individuals have no real market for small parcels of voluntary credits, and the firm dissolves or offers an 'exit' for another fee.

carbon-credit-scam.whyItWorks: Carbon markets are real and appear in the news, but almost nobody knows how credits are priced or traded. Buying something that claims to protect rainforest lets an investor feel principled, which dulls the questions they would ask about any other commodity.

realVsFake.real: Carbon credits are bought in bulk by companies offsetting emissions, through specialist brokers and registries.
realVsFake.fake: Retail savers are sold a few hundred credits each as a personal investment, with a brochure about soaring demand.

realVsFake.real: A regulated investment firm states that capital is at risk and names the market where you can sell.
realVsFake.fake: The pitch guarantees double-digit growth and brushes off resale questions with talk of a buyer already lined up.

realVsFake.real: Credits on a recognised registry can be looked up by serial number, showing the project and current holder.
realVsFake.fake: You receive a decorative certificate, but the serials are absent from the registry or already marked as retired.

steps.title: Details copied somewhere else
steps.detail: The long card number, expiry date and three-digit code are captured by a fake delivery-fee page, a hacked shop checkout, or bought from a leaked batch.

steps.title: A tiny test charge
steps.detail: An automated script tries the card for a pound or two at a charity donation page or a digital download store, to see whether it is live.

steps.title: The spending run
steps.detail: If it clears, larger orders follow fast: electronics, food delivery credit, gaming top-ups. Merchants that skip the extra bank approval step are chosen on purpose.

steps.title: Getting past the passcode
steps.detail: Where a one-time code is required, the fraudster rings or texts you posing as the bank and asks you to read it out to 'cancel' the purchase.

card-not-present-scam.whyItWorks: Online shops need only the numbers printed on the card, so the plastic never has to leave your wallet. A charge of a pound or two is easy to overlook among everyday spending, which buys the criminal time.

realVsFake.real: Your own online purchases come from retailers you recognise, at times you were actually shopping.
realVsFake.fake: Charges appear overnight from merchants abroad, or with names made of random letters.

realVsFake.real: A bank's fraud alert asks you to reply yes or no, or to check its app. It does not ask for the code.
realVsFake.fake: A caller says a code is on its way and that reading it back will stop the purchase.

realVsFake.real: If a delivery charge is genuinely owed, the courier's own app or the driver at the door takes it.
realVsFake.fake: A text demands a small redelivery fee, and the page wants every digit on your card plus your date of birth.

steps.title: Points about to lapse
steps.detail: A text or call in the card issuer's name says several thousand reward points, worth a couple of hundred in cashback, will be wiped at midnight.

steps.title: The helpful redemption desk
steps.detail: An agent offers to convert the points into a voucher right now and 'just needs to locate your card', asking for the sixteen digits and expiry.

steps.title: A copy of the rewards catalogue
steps.detail: Alternatively a link opens a page of gifts and vouchers, asking you to sign in with your card login and enter the CVV to 'credit the cashback'.

steps.title: The OTP that 'credits' you
steps.detail: A code arrives and the agent says reading it out confirms the redemption. It is in fact approving a purchase or transfer they have just set up.

card-rewards-scam.whyItWorks: Reward points feel like money you have already earned, so losing them stings more than missing a random prize. Since cardholders rarely check their points balance, almost any figure quoted sounds about right.

realVsFake.real: Card issuers show your points balance and expiry date in their app or on your statement, and you redeem there yourself.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger phones to do the redemption for you and wants the card number read out.

realVsFake.real: Redeeming points never needs a one-time passcode, because nothing is being paid out of your account.
realVsFake.fake: The agent says a code must be shared to 'release' the cashback onto your card.

realVsFake.real: Loyalty schemes that expire points usually flag it on statements well ahead of time.
realVsFake.fake: The first you hear of any expiry is a message giving you until tonight.

steps.title: The overlay goes on
steps.detail: A moulded plastic reader is clipped over the real card slot, or a wafer-thin 'shimmer' is pushed inside it. Fitting takes under a minute.

steps.title: Capturing the PIN
steps.detail: A pinhole camera hidden in a strip above the screen or in a leaflet holder films the keys, or a false keypad laid on top records each press.

steps.title: Your transaction works normally
steps.detail: Cash comes out, fuel pumps, the receipt prints. Nothing seems wrong, because the genuine reader underneath still does its job while the copy is made.

steps.title: Clones and cash-outs
steps.detail: The gang collects the device, writes the stolen data onto blank cards and withdraws cash, often in another country or at machines that still read magnetic stripes.

card-skimming-scam.whyItWorks: Nothing unusual happens at the time, so there is no moment that feels like a scam and nothing to refuse. People trust a machine bolted to a bank wall or a forecourt pump and rarely tug at its parts before using it.

realVsFake.real: A genuine card slot sits flush with the fascia, and its flashing light surround is fully visible.
realVsFake.fake: A skimmer stands proud of the panel, covers the light, and may wobble if you pull it.

realVsFake.real: Factory keypads are firm and sit level with the metal around them.
realVsFake.fake: A false pad feels thick or spongy, and the keys may stand higher than the casing.

realVsFake.real: Many fuel stations seal pump doors with security tape that stays in one piece.
realVsFake.fake: On a tampered pump the tape is cut, missing, or shows a 'void' pattern across the door.

steps.title: Activate secure payments
steps.detail: An email with Visa or Mastercard marks beside a bank logo says new rules require enrolling your card in 3-D Secure, or online purchases will be declined.

steps.title: The enrolment form
steps.detail: The page asks for the sixteen-digit number, expiry date, security code, name and date of birth, and sometimes the card's PIN.

steps.title: We have sent you a code
steps.detail: While you wait, the criminals are entering your card at a real shop or adding it to a phone wallet. The code your bank texts is for that.

steps.title: Successfully verified
steps.detail: You type the code and a green tick appears. Their purchase goes through, or your card becomes active for tap payments on a stranger's phone.

card-verification-email-scam.whyItWorks: Shoppers meet extra bank check screens at checkout without ever being told how they were set up. An email offering to activate that protection sounds like the missing instruction, and it borrows the card schemes' names.

realVsFake.real: Card security checks are switched on by your bank automatically and appear only during a purchase you are making.
realVsFake.fake: An email asks you to enrol in advance by filling in a form.

realVsFake.real: The bank's text states what the code is for, naming the shop and amount or the wallet being set up.
realVsFake.fake: The page calls it a 'verification code' and counts on you not reading the text closely.

realVsFake.real: No bank asks for a card PIN on a website or by email.
realVsFake.fake: The form includes a PIN box, labelled as identity confirmation.

steps.title: Login details phished in advance
steps.detail: A fake bank text or lookalike sign-in page has already captured your username and password. The fraudster now lacks one thing needed to enrol a device.

steps.title: A new handset joins your account
steps.detail: They add your card to a mobile wallet or register the banking app on their phone, which makes your bank text you a verification code.

steps.title: 'Security' on the line
steps.detail: At that moment a caller says a cardless withdrawal is being attempted in another city and asks for the code to block it.

steps.title: Tap and withdraw
steps.detail: With the code, their phone becomes your card. They hold it to a contactless cash machine, or generate a cash code in the app, and withdraw up to the daily limit.

cardless-atm-scam.whyItWorks: The code really does arrive from the bank's usual number at the instant the caller mentions it, which seems to prove the caller is genuine. Most customers have never used cardless cash, so they cannot tell that the code switches it on.

realVsFake.real: A cardless withdrawal starts in your own banking app, on your phone, while you are standing at the machine.
realVsFake.fake: An alert or code about cardless cash arrives while you are at home and have not opened the app.

realVsFake.real: Bank texts carrying a code state its purpose, such as adding a card to a wallet or registering a device.
realVsFake.fake: The caller describes the same code as a 'cancellation reference' and talks over you as you read the message.

realVsFake.real: To stop a suspicious withdrawal, a bank blocks it internally and may ask you to confirm inside the app.
realVsFake.fake: The 'security team' claims the block cannot go through unless you say the digits aloud.

steps.title: The #blessing post
steps.detail: A social media account running a 'Cash App Friday' style giveaway replies that you have won, or a stranger messages that they are 'blessing' followers today.

steps.title: A small send to 'verify'
steps.detail: You are asked to send 20 or so to a cashtag to prove your account is active, with a promise that it will come back multiplied.

steps.title: A screenshot of 'pending' money
steps.detail: They send a doctored image showing hundreds waiting for you, and say a 'clearance fee' or account upgrade is needed to release it.

steps.title: 'Support' wants the sign-in code
steps.detail: When you complain, a fake support account or phone number offers help and requests your sign-in code or PIN, then logs in and empties the balance.

cash-app-scam.whyItWorks: The company has run genuine giveaways on social media, so the hashtag and the format are familiar. Sending twenty to receive hundreds seems a tiny risk, and payments in the app go through instantly with no way to pull them back.

realVsFake.real: Cash App's real giveaways are announced from its verified accounts, and winners are never asked to send money first.
realVsFake.fake: A lookalike profile with extra letters in its name messages you privately asking for a 'verification' payment.

realVsFake.real: Genuine support is reached through the app's own help section, and staff never ask for your PIN or sign-in code.
realVsFake.fake: 'Support' is a phone number from a search advert or a reply under your complaint, and its first request is your code.

realVsFake.real: Someone who really paid the wrong person can ask the app's support team to sort it out.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger sends money from a stolen card, begs you to send it back, and the original is later reversed.

steps.title: A livestream with a famous face
steps.detail: A video stream on a hijacked or renamed channel replays old interview footage of a tech billionaire, framed with a banner announcing a giveaway to mark a launch.

steps.title: The QR code in the corner
steps.detail: Viewers are pointed to a site through a QR code or pinned comment. It shows the rules: send between 0.1 and 5 BTC and receive twice as much back.

steps.title: A scrolling list of 'winners'
steps.detail: The page displays a live table of incoming and outgoing transactions and a countdown of remaining places. Chat is full of bot accounts thanking the host.

steps.title: One-way transfer
steps.detail: You send coins to the address shown. Nothing returns, the transaction cannot be recalled, and the page may suggest sending again because the first amount was 'below the minimum'.

celebrity-crypto-giveaway-scam.whyItWorks: The footage is real, the channel may carry a verification badge and a large subscriber count, and wealthy founders are known for publicity stunts. A fake transaction feed showing strangers apparently being paid makes the remaining slots feel like they are slipping away.

realVsFake.real: Real promotions from crypto companies credit existing customers' accounts and never need you to send coins first.
realVsFake.fake: The giveaway only pays after a 'verification deposit' to an address shown on screen.

realVsFake.real: A public figure's genuine announcement appears on every one of their established accounts and in mainstream news.
realVsFake.fake: The event exists on one channel whose older videos are about gaming or music in another language.

realVsFake.real: A live broadcast responds to events and takes questions as they come in.
realVsFake.fake: The 'live' video loops every few minutes, and comments are switched off or limited to long-standing subscribers.

steps.title: Homework on your company
steps.detail: The scammer reads the company website and LinkedIn to learn who the boss is, who handles payments, who has just joined and when the boss is away.

steps.title: Are you at your desk?
steps.detail: A short email arrives under the chief executive's name from a free mail account or lookalike domain, asking only whether you are available for a quick favour.

steps.title: The discreet task
steps.detail: Once you reply, the request lands: buy four gift cards for clients, or pay an attached invoice to a new supplier today, and keep it confidential.

steps.title: Codes photographed, wire sent
steps.detail: You scratch the cards and email pictures of the codes, or finance sends the transfer to a mule account. The 'boss' stops replying and the money moves on.

ceo-fraud-scam.whyItWorks: Refusing the boss carries a cost that agreeing to an odd request does not, particularly for a new starter. The first email asks only whether you are free, so by the time money is mentioned you have already said yes.

realVsFake.real: A genuine payment request from an executive goes through purchasing, with a purchase order and a second approver.
realVsFake.fake: The email asks you to skip approvals 'just this once' and mention it to nobody.

realVsFake.real: Real bosses can be reached on a known number, on the company chat or through their assistant.
realVsFake.fake: The sender is in back-to-back meetings or boarding a flight, and tells you not to phone.

realVsFake.real: Companies buy client gifts on a company card, with receipts filed afterwards.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to pay from your own pocket, scratch the panels and send photos of the codes.

steps.title: A lookalike in the store
steps.detail: You search for a well-known AI assistant and the top result is a sponsored app with a near-identical icon and a name one word off.

steps.title: The trial screen with a hidden X
steps.detail: On first launch a full-screen offer appears. The close button is faint or delayed, so most people tap 'Continue' and start a three-day trial.

steps.title: Permissions a chat app never needs
steps.detail: It requests contacts, storage, notifications and sometimes accessibility access. The chat itself gives a few short answers, then hits a daily limit.

steps.title: Weekly billing begins
steps.detail: After three days the store bills you every week, which over a month costs more than the genuine tool's paid plan. Deleting the app does not cancel it.

chatgpt-app-scam.whyItWorks: People have heard of the famous AI tools but often do not know who makes them or what the official app is called. A familiar-looking icon near the top of a store search is enough to pass for the genuine article.

realVsFake.real: The genuine assistant is published under the AI company's own name and linked from that company's official website.
realVsFake.fake: The developer is an unknown studio whose other listings are wallpaper, scanner and phone-cleaner apps.

realVsFake.real: Well-known chatbots have a usable free tier and show monthly pricing on a settings page.
realVsFake.fake: A paywall appears before your second question, with the price in small grey print under a large button.

realVsFake.real: A text chat app needs a network connection, plus a microphone only if you choose voice input.
realVsFake.fake: It wants your contacts, files and permission to draw over other apps before you type anything.

steps.title: Cash today, no bank needed
steps.detail: A flyer, shopfront sign or social media advert offers instant money for payroll, benefit or insurance cheques, aimed at people without a bank account or in a hurry.

steps.title: Endorse it and hand it over
steps.detail: You are asked to sign the back of the cheque and post it, photograph both sides, or leave it at a counter, along with a copy of your ID.

steps.title: Deductions nobody mentioned
steps.detail: The payout arrives short. A 'verification charge', a 'same-day premium' and a 'risk fee' have been taken, sometimes swallowing a large slice of the cheque's value.

steps.title: Or no payout at all
steps.detail: In the worst version the phone number goes dead. The signed cheque has been paid into someone else's account and your ID copy is reused elsewhere.

cheque-cashing-scam.whyItWorks: A paper cheque is awkward for anyone with no bank account, or with an overdraft that would swallow it, and waiting days for clearance is hard when rent is due. A stranger offering notes in hand today solves an immediate problem.

realVsFake.real: A licensed cheque casher displays its fee as a clear rate on the wall and on a receipt before you sign anything.
realVsFake.fake: The cost is described as 'a small fee' and only becomes a number once they hold your cheque.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate service pays you across the counter during the same visit, and you leave with paperwork.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to post the cheque or send photos and wait for a deposit that may never come.

realVsFake.real: Your own bank, or the bank that issued the cheque, will usually cash or deposit it for little or nothing.
realVsFake.fake: The service warns that banks will 'hold it for weeks' and pushes you to decide on the spot.

steps.title: Lifted from the post
steps.detail: A thief fishes envelopes from a street postbox with a sticky line, raids a building's outgoing mail tray, or takes bill payments left out for collection.

steps.title: The solvent bath
steps.detail: The cheque is soaked in a household chemical such as nail varnish remover. Ordinary ballpoint ink dissolves, while the printed details and often your signature remain.

steps.title: A new payee, a bigger figure
steps.detail: Once dry, the blank spaces are filled in with a different name and a larger amount, or the cheque is scanned to print further forgeries.

steps.title: Paid in through a borrowed account
steps.detail: The altered cheque is deposited by phone app or at a machine, into an account opened with false ID or lent by a recruited 'money mule', then withdrawn fast.

cheque-washing-scam.whyItWorks: There is no persuasion here at all. The cheque carries your real signature, account number and the bank's own paper, so it passes automated checks, and you only find out when the intended recipient chases you for payment.

realVsFake.real: The cheque image in your banking app should show your own handwriting, the payee you named and the amount you wrote.
realVsFake.fake: A washed cheque shows a different hand or pen in the payee and amount lines, with your signature untouched.

realVsFake.real: A payee who receives your cheque banks it and stops asking for payment.
realVsFake.fake: Your statement shows the cheque as paid, yet the company you posted it to sends a reminder.

realVsFake.real: Ink from a pigmented gel pen soaks into the paper fibres and resists solvents.
realVsFake.fake: Washers look for cheques written in standard ballpoint, which lifts off cleanly and leaves little trace.

steps.title: Mining without the machines
steps.detail: An advert, messaging group or friend's referral link promotes a site that rents out mining power, promising a fixed payout every day with no hardware or electricity bill.

steps.title: The starter contract
steps.detail: You buy a 300 starter contract in crypto. Photos of a server hall and a 'hash rate' figure appear in your new account.

steps.title: A counter that ticks up daily
steps.detail: The dashboard credits earnings each morning. A small first withdrawal is paid promptly, which encourages a bigger contract and invitations to friends for a referral bonus.

steps.title: Withdrawal needs an upgrade
steps.detail: A larger withdrawal is refused until you reach a higher membership tier or pay a 'network tax'. Paying brings a new condition, then the site goes offline.

cloud-mining-scam.whyItWorks: Mining is known to be profitable for those with warehouses of equipment, so renting a share sounds reasonable. That early small withdrawal is paid from other people's deposits and does the persuading: it looks like proof the machines exist.

realVsFake.real: Actual mining income rises and falls with coin price, network difficulty and power costs, and can be negative.
realVsFake.fake: The contract pays the same amount every day regardless of what the market does.

realVsFake.real: A genuine hosting company names its data centre, its legal entity and the mining pool where payouts can be seen.
realVsFake.fake: The site shows stock photos of server racks, an address that turns out to be a shared office, and no pool records.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate services take their charges out of what you have earned before paying you the rest.
realVsFake.fake: You must send fresh crypto from outside to cover a fee, even though the balance on screen is many times larger.

steps.title: Your address is on a list
steps.detail: Names and addresses come from leaked shopping data. Sometimes a text arrives the day before, saying an order is out for delivery and to keep cash ready.

steps.title: A genuine courier knocks
steps.detail: The driver works for a real delivery firm and knows nothing. The label carries a family member's name and a cash-on-delivery amount such as 35.

steps.title: Pay before you open
steps.detail: The driver says the box cannot be opened before payment. A parent or flatmate, assuming somebody in the house ordered it, hands over the cash or taps a card.

steps.title: Tissue paper in a box
steps.detail: Inside is a cheap trinket or crumpled packing. The sender's number is disconnected, and the delivery firm passes your payment to the seller as it would for any order.

cod-parcel-scam.whyItWorks: Households share one front door, so whoever answers assumes someone else placed the order. Turning a driver away feels ruder and riskier than paying a modest sum, and the courier on the step is entirely real.

realVsFake.real: With a genuine order, somebody in the house chose to pay on delivery at checkout and has a confirmation naming the seller.
realVsFake.fake: Nobody can find an order, and the label's sender is a mobile number or a vague trading name.

realVsFake.real: Delivery firms accept a refusal. An unpaid parcel simply travels back to whoever sent it, at no cost to you.
realVsFake.fake: The scheme depends on the driver's hurry and your worry that refusing causes trouble for a relative.

realVsFake.real: A real seller answers the phone number printed on the label and can quote what was bought.
realVsFake.fake: The return address is half complete and the number rings out or is switched off.

steps.title: Dear esteemed Doctor
steps.detail: A flattering email cites one of your papers or your LinkedIn profile and invites you to give a keynote at an 'international summit' in a famous city.

steps.title: A website full of borrowed logos
steps.detail: The event site lists a grand scientific committee, university and sponsor logos used without permission, and a hotel venue. The programme itself stays vague.

steps.title: Registration, visa letter, hotel block
steps.detail: Confirming your slot means a speaker registration fee, then a charge for a visa invitation letter and a hotel booking through their agent, plus a passport scan.

steps.title: No podium at the end
steps.detail: After payment by transfer the organiser goes silent, or the 'summit' is a hired room holding a few other paying speakers. The passport copy is kept for reuse.

conference-invite-email-scam.whyItWorks: Being asked to speak is a professional compliment people want to believe, and academics and founders are under real pressure to present abroad. Genuine conferences charge registration too, so the first invoice does not look strange.

realVsFake.real: Established conferences choose speakers through a call for papers or a committee member who knows your field.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger offers a keynote slot to anyone who replies, then sends a bill for it.

realVsFake.real: Real events have past editions, recorded talks and named organisers at a society or company you can telephone.
realVsFake.fake: The organiser runs dozens of near-identical 'world congress' sites, and listed committee members have never heard of it.

realVsFake.real: You apply for a visa yourself at the embassy or its official service, and book hotels directly.
realVsFake.fake: The organiser insists its 'travel desk' handles both, and needs a passport scan and bank transfer first.

steps.title: A card or phone disappears
steps.detail: It is lifted from a pocket in a crowd, left in a taxi, or snatched from a pub table. Sometimes only the card is slipped out of a wallet.

steps.title: A burst of small taps
steps.detail: The thief makes quick purchases under the contactless limit at vending machines, transport gates, self-checkouts and corner shops, where nobody looks at the name on the card.

steps.title: Buying things to resell
steps.detail: Tobacco, alcohol, travel top-ups and gift cards are favourites. They move between shops so that no single terminal asks for the PIN.

steps.title: Loading it onto a wallet
steps.detail: Some try to add the card to their own phone's wallet, which needs a code from your bank. A phishing text or call to you often follows.

contactless-card-theft-scam.whyItWorks: Tap payments under the limit need no PIN and no signature, a convenience the thief inherits the second the card changes hands. Each purchase is small enough to pass for normal spending until the owner checks.

realVsFake.real: Your own tap payments match where you were: your station, your supermarket, your lunch stop.
realVsFake.fake: A string of charges appears from shops you never visited, minutes apart, starting soon after you last saw the card.

realVsFake.real: A bank message about adding your card to a wallet arrives because you are setting up your own phone.
realVsFake.fake: A 'wallet activation' code arrives unprompted, sometimes followed by someone asking you to pass it on.

realVsFake.real: Freezing a card in the banking app takes seconds and can be undone if it turns up.
realVsFake.fake: The thief counts on you spending an hour retracing your steps before you think of blocking it.

steps.title: A trader's lifestyle feed
steps.detail: A social media account posts profit screenshots, hired sports cars and beach laptops. A link in the bio invites followers to 'copy my trades and earn while you sleep'.

steps.title: Sign up through his link
steps.detail: In a private chat the 'master trader' tells you to register on one particular platform using his code, which he says is the only place the mirroring works.

steps.title: Switch on auto-copy
steps.detail: You deposit and enable copying. The account shows a run of winning trades matching his posts, and he suggests adding funds to reach the 'pro tier' with bigger positions.

steps.title: One bad trade, or a profit share
steps.detail: Either a single 'liquidation' wipes the balance overnight, or a withdrawal is held until you pay the trader's performance cut in advance from your own pocket.

copy-trading-scam.whyItWorks: Copy trading is a real feature on regulated brokers, so the idea is familiar. It appeals to people who believe trading profits exist but doubt their own skill, and a leaderboard of someone else's wins seems to remove the need to learn anything.

realVsFake.real: On a regulated broker, a trader's full history is published, including losing months and the deepest drawdown.
realVsFake.fake: The record consists of cropped screenshots, and losing trades never appear in the feed or on the leaderboard.

realVsFake.real: Genuine copy features let you choose among many traders and stop copying with one click.
realVsFake.fake: You are steered to a single website nobody has reviewed, reachable only through the trader's personal invitation link.

realVsFake.real: Any performance fee on a real platform is deducted automatically from realised profit.
realVsFake.fake: The trader asks you to send his share directly, in crypto, before the platform will release your funds.

steps.title: A landline call about cloning
steps.detail: The caller, often targeting older people at home, says he is from the bank's fraud unit or a police station and that your card was copied at a local shop.

steps.title: The fake call-back check
steps.detail: To prove it, he invites you to hang up and dial the bank. He keeps the line open, plays a dial tone, and an accomplice 'answers' as the bank.

steps.title: PIN typed into the handset
steps.detail: You are asked to key your PIN on the phone keypad 'so the system can cancel it', or to write it on a slip and seal it with the card.

steps.title: A knock at the door
steps.detail: A smartly dressed courier or taxi driver, sometimes hired innocently, arrives with a password you were given and takes the envelope. The card is used within the hour.

courier-card-collection-scam.whyItWorks: Offering a call-back check makes the caller seem scrupulous, and few people know that some landlines stay connected when only one side hangs up. A courier at the door with the agreed password then looks like the bank being thorough.

realVsFake.real: When a card is compromised, the bank cancels it remotely and posts a replacement. The old one can be cut up.
realVsFake.fake: The caller insists the 'cloned' card is evidence and must be collected intact.

realVsFake.real: No bank or police officer ever sends someone to your home for a card, cash or valuables.
realVsFake.fake: A collection is booked for the same afternoon, and you are given a secret word to exchange on the doorstep.

realVsFake.real: Your PIN is never needed to cancel a card, and bank staff will not ask for it.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to enter it on the telephone keypad or put it in the envelope for 'verification at the depot'.

steps.title: The 'clean slate' pitch
steps.detail: A radio advert, flyer or social media post promises to erase defaults, late payments and court judgments from your credit file within thirty days.

steps.title: Payment before any work
steps.detail: A consultant takes a sign-up charge of several hundred plus a monthly retainer, and asks for your ID and full access to your credit reports.

steps.title: Disputing everything
steps.detail: They flood the credit reference agencies with template letters claiming accurate debts are not yours. Entries may vanish briefly while under review, then return.

steps.title: The 'new identity' trick
steps.detail: Some go further and sell you a fresh nine-digit number or tell you to apply using altered details, which is itself fraud committed in your name.

credit-repair-scam.whyItWorks: A poor score blocks mortgages, rentals and phone contracts, and the rules behind it feel opaque, so a specialist claiming inside knowledge sounds worth paying. A temporary dip in negative entries during disputes looks like early proof it is working.

realVsFake.real: Credit reference agencies let you dispute a genuine error yourself for free, and must investigate it.
realVsFake.fake: The firm says only its 'legal team' can talk to the agencies and tells you not to contact them.

realVsFake.real: A reputable adviser explains that correct negative information stays on file until it ages off.
realVsFake.fake: The salesperson guarantees a set points increase and removal of debts you really do owe.

realVsFake.real: Free debt charities and honest advisers charge nothing upfront, or bill only once a service has been delivered.
realVsFake.fake: Money is taken on day one by card or transfer, with a retainer that continues whether or not anything changes.

steps.title: Tokens or a tag out of nowhere
steps.detail: A direct message, a reply under a project's post, or an unknown token appearing in your wallet announces that your address qualifies for an airdrop.

steps.title: A claim page with a timer
steps.detail: The link opens a copy of the project's site, with the right logo and a domain one character off. A clock shows hours remaining to claim.

steps.title: Connect, then sign
steps.detail: Pressing 'Claim' opens your wallet with a signature request. The text is a block of code, or an approval giving the site's contract spending rights over your tokens.

steps.title: A drainer script empties it
steps.detail: Seconds after you confirm, an automated script sweeps your most valuable coins and NFTs to another address. No free tokens ever arrive.

crypto-airdrop-scam.whyItWorks: Genuine airdrops have handed early users valuable tokens for nothing, and claiming those did involve connecting a wallet. Because no money is requested and a signature feels like a login, people confirm a request they cannot read.

realVsFake.real: A real project announces an airdrop on its long-standing official channels, with eligibility rules published in advance.
realVsFake.fake: News of the drop reaches you by private message from an account posing as a moderator or support helper.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate claim transaction sends tokens to you and costs only the network fee.
realVsFake.fake: The prompt requests permission over tokens you already hold, such as 'set approval for all' or an unlimited spend.

realVsFake.real: Surprise tokens from a genuine distribution can be ignored safely and need no website visit.
realVsFake.fake: The mystery token's name is itself a web address, telling you to visit it to swap or unlock the reward.

steps.title: An email from 'customs clearance'
steps.detail: The message carries a postal or courier logo and a subject like 'Shipment on hold: duty unpaid', with a reference that resembles a tracking code.

steps.title: The itemised charge
steps.detail: A neat table lists import VAT, a handling fee and a total of 3.50, with a warning that daily storage costs begin after 48 hours.

steps.title: The 'Pay duty' button
steps.detail: The button leads to a payment form on an unrelated domain asking for your name, home address, phone number and full card details.

steps.title: A fake bank approval screen
steps.detail: A mock 3-D Secure page requests the code your bank just texted. That code actually approves a far larger purchase, or adds your card to a criminal's phone wallet.

customs-duty-email-scam.whyItWorks: Import charges on overseas orders are real, and most shoppers have no idea how much to expect or who collects them. A table of VAT lines totalling a few coins looks like routine bureaucracy.

realVsFake.real: Real duty is worked out from the declared value of a specific item, and the notice quotes a tracking number that works.
realVsFake.fake: The email names no sender, country or item, and the fee is a suspiciously tiny figure.

realVsFake.real: The carrier collects import charges through its own website or app, by letter, or at the door.
realVsFake.fake: An emailed button sends you to a card form hosted somewhere with no connection to the carrier.

realVsFake.real: Parcels awaiting duty are generally kept for many days, with a reminder sent before anything is returned.
realVsFake.fake: You are told the goods will be destroyed or returned within two days.

steps.title: A request you never made
steps.detail: An email says your account data download is ready, imitating the export notices sent by Google, Facebook or Instagram when someone asks for a copy of their data.

steps.title: Two buttons, one destination
steps.detail: It offers 'Download file' and 'Wasn't you? Secure your account'. Both lead to the same counterfeit page, so curiosity and caution end in the same place.

steps.title: Sign in to retrieve the archive
steps.detail: The page mimics the 're-enter your password to continue' step that genuine exports use, then asks for the code sent to your phone.

steps.title: The export becomes real
