steps.detail: With your login, attackers can request the true archive holding every message, photo and contact, or change the password and lock you out.

data-download-email-scam.whyItWorks: The email works in two directions. Curious people want to see the file, while cautious people fear someone else has asked for their data, and both groups reach for a button leading to one password form.

realVsFake.real: A genuine export exists only because you asked for it in account settings, and the notice follows that request.
realVsFake.fake: The email turns up with no request behind it and a 24-hour expiry.

realVsFake.real: Real services list pending and completed exports on a settings page you can open yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The only way offered to see the file is the button in the email.

realVsFake.real: Genuine security notices give the device, rough location and time of the activity.
realVsFake.fake: It says 'a request was received' and gives no device, place or time at all.

steps.title: A newly listed company gets a letter
steps.detail: Soon after incorporation, a letter or email headed with a regulator-style logo says the business has not registered as a data controller.

steps.title: Fines quoted in bold
steps.detail: It cites data protection law, mentions penalties running to thousands, and gives a compliance reference so it reads like an enforcement notice.

steps.title: A fee several times too high
steps.detail: The registration charge shown is well above the regulator's real tier for a small firm, sometimes padded with a 'certificate' or 'compliance pack'.

steps.title: Paid to a look-alike 'registry'
steps.detail: Payment goes by card on a copycat site or by transfer to a limited company. At best the firm is registered at a mark-up, at worst nothing is filed.

data-protection-fee-scam.whyItWorks: Many small businesses do owe a data protection fee and have never heard of it, so the demand contains a grain of truth. A new director facing a letter about GDPR fines would sooner pay a modest sum than read the legislation.

realVsFake.real: The data protection regulator publishes its fee tiers and a free self-assessment showing whether you need to pay at all.
realVsFake.fake: The notice assumes every business must pay and quotes one flat price with no mention of exemptions.

realVsFake.real: Payment is made on the regulator's own website, and the business then appears on its public register of fee payers.
realVsFake.fake: The payee is a company with 'data', 'registration' or 'compliance' in its name and a mailbox address.

realVsFake.real: A regulator's reminder gives a reference you can check by ringing its published helpline.
realVsFake.fake: A caller follows up within days offering to take card details over the phone to 'stop the fine being issued'.

steps.title: One lower monthly payment
steps.detail: A cold call, advert or official-looking letter offers a 'government-backed relief programme' that rolls credit cards and loans into a single reduced payment.

steps.title: Stop paying your creditors
steps.detail: The adviser tells you to cancel direct debits to lenders and not to answer their calls, saying the firm now speaks for you.

steps.title: Money goes into their account
steps.detail: You set up a monthly payment to the company. The first several instalments are kept as 'set-up' and 'administration' charges, and nothing is passed on.

steps.title: Arrears, defaults and court letters
steps.detail: Months later your lenders write about missed payments, added interest and legal action. The firm's line is disconnected, or it blames you for 'breaking the plan'.

debt-consolidation-scam.whyItWorks: Someone juggling several creditors badly wants the calls to stop, and 'we will deal with them for you' offers exactly that. Being told not to speak to lenders hides the damage until it is serious.

realVsFake.real: A genuine consolidation loan pays off your old lenders directly, and you can see those balances drop to zero.
realVsFake.fake: Your creditors hear nothing, receive nothing, and your statements with them keep growing.

realVsFake.real: Free debt advice charities set up managed plans without charging and send statements of what each creditor received.
realVsFake.fake: The company keeps your early payments as fees and never produces a breakdown.

realVsFake.real: Honest advisers tell you to keep talking to lenders and warn that reduced payments will affect your credit file.
realVsFake.fake: You are instructed to ignore creditor letters and promised that half the debt will simply be written off.

steps.title: A message from the top
steps.detail: A finance employee receives an email or WhatsApp in the chief executive's name about a confidential acquisition, saying a lawyer will be in touch and to tell nobody.

steps.title: The meeting invitation
steps.detail: A calendar invite follows for a video call. On screen are the executive and sometimes other familiar colleagues, all generated from public interviews and conference footage.

steps.title: Instructions, then a quick exit
steps.detail: The fake executive speaks briefly, gives the amount and beneficiary, blames a poor connection and leaves. Any questions are pushed to chat or email.

steps.title: Payments in several slices
steps.detail: Staff send the transfer, often split into smaller payments to stay under approval limits, to a newly opened company account abroad. It is emptied within hours.

deepfake-ceo-scam.whyItWorks: Employees are trained to distrust odd emails, but seeing and hearing the boss on a call feels like the verification itself. Being chosen for a secret deal is flattering, and nobody wants to be the person who delayed it.

realVsFake.real: A genuine executive expects large payments to pass the usual dual sign-off, even for a deal still under wraps.
realVsFake.fake: The caller says the normal approvers must not be told, citing confidentiality rules around the deal.

realVsFake.real: On a live call a real person can turn their head, hold up a hand, or answer an unexpected question about last week.
realVsFake.fake: The face stays front-on and still, speech is short and scripted, and the call ends before anyone can probe.

realVsFake.real: Proper payment instructions arrive through the company's finance system, for a beneficiary already on file.
realVsFake.fake: Account details are pasted into the meeting chat or sent from a personal email, for a payee nobody has paid before.

steps.title: An advert between ordinary posts
steps.detail: A sponsored video shows a familiar entrepreneur or news presenter, apparently mid-interview, describing an automated trading platform that ordinary people can join.

steps.title: A cloned news article
steps.detail: Clicking leads to a page dressed as a national newspaper or broadcaster, with a headline about banks trying to suppress the system and a registration box.

steps.title: The call centre rings back
steps.detail: Minutes after you enter a phone number, an 'investment adviser' calls. He takes a 250 starting deposit by card and sets up a trading account for you.

steps.title: Bigger deposits, then a locked account
steps.detail: The account shows quick gains, and the adviser pushes for thousands more, sometimes via screen sharing. Requests to withdraw are met with tax demands and silence.

deepfake-investment-scam.whyItWorks: People trust what they see and hear, and a cloned voice saying the words in the right accent beats any written testimonial. The setting helps too: the clip sits inside a familiar feed, styled like a news interview the viewer half remembers.

realVsFake.real: Well-known business figures promote their own companies through official channels and do not front retail trading schemes.
realVsFake.fake: The clip appears only as a paid advert from a page with a random name and a handful of followers.

realVsFake.real: A genuine interview can be found in full on the broadcaster's own site, with the same words in context.
realVsFake.fake: The mouth drifts out of time with the voice, the face blurs when the head turns, and the original footage is about something else.

realVsFake.real: News organisations report on investments without sign-up forms and do not collect phone numbers for brokers.
realVsFake.fake: Every link on the fake article, including the menu and the weather, leads to the same registration form.

steps.title: A new pool with a huge rate
steps.detail: A group chat post, sponsored tweet or 'alpha' message promotes a freshly launched liquidity pool paying a fixed daily reward, with an audit badge on the homepage.

steps.title: Approve the staking contract
steps.detail: To stake, your wallet asks you to approve the contract for your stablecoins. The allowance is preset to unlimited, far more than the amount you plan to put in.

steps.title: Rewards pile up on screen
steps.detail: The farm page shows your stake and a reward figure climbing by the hour. A notice says the pool is nearly full, nudging you to add more.

steps.title: The contract owner pulls the funds
steps.detail: Using the allowance, the developers move your staked tokens and anything else of that type left in your wallet. The 'harvest' button fails and the site vanishes.

defi-yield-scam.whyItWorks: Early yield farms really did pay startling rates for a short while, so a high figure does not look impossible to someone who missed out. Approval prompts are routine in DeFi, and experienced users click them many times a week without reading the allowance.

realVsFake.real: Established protocols publish audited, verified contract code, and their yields move with market conditions.
realVsFake.fake: The audit badge links nowhere or to a firm that has never heard of the project, and the daily rate never changes.

realVsFake.real: A sound staking contract lets you set an allowance equal to your deposit and withdraw the stake yourself.
realVsFake.fake: Lowering the allowance makes the page throw an error, and withdrawal depends on a function only the owner can call.

realVsFake.real: Reputable projects have named or long-known developers and a history visible on a block explorer.
realVsFake.fake: The contract was deployed days ago by an anonymous team, and questions in the group chat get the asker banned.

steps.title: Verify your delivery account
steps.detail: An email or text says new security rules mean your courier account must be verified, or your saved delivery preferences will be wiped.

steps.title: The cloned app login
steps.detail: The link opens a browser copy of the courier's sign-in page, asking for your email, your password and then the code sent to your phone.

steps.title: A look around your account
steps.detail: Logged in to the real account, the thief can see saved addresses, your phone number, parcels currently on their way and sometimes a stored payment card.

steps.title: Parcels quietly diverted
steps.detail: Incoming deliveries are redirected to a pickup shop. The notification email is changed so you hear nothing, and the same password is tried on your email and shopping accounts.

delivery-app-phishing-scam.whyItWorks: A courier account seems to have no money in it, so people guard it less carefully than a bank login. The threat of deliveries stopping is enough to make one more sign-in feel like housekeeping.

realVsFake.real: Courier apps keep you signed in, and any security check happens inside the app you already have installed.
realVsFake.fake: A message pushes you to a web page to sign in again from scratch.

realVsFake.real: A genuine diversion request triggers a notice to the email and phone already on file.
realVsFake.fake: After a takeover the contact details are changed first, so every warning goes to the thief.

realVsFake.real: Delivery preferences such as a safe place are optional extras that nobody is penalised for skipping.
realVsFake.fake: The message claims your account will be deactivated and parcels refused unless you verify today.

steps.title: The thank-you message
steps.detail: Soon after a delivery, or at random, a text thanks you for your recent order and offers a reward for a thirty-second survey.

steps.title: Three easy questions
steps.detail: Was the parcel on time, was the driver polite, how many stars. A progress bar fills and a counter shows only a few rewards left.

steps.title: Pick a gift box
steps.detail: A grid of nine boxes appears. Your first choice is empty, your second 'wins' a phone or air fryer, and glowing comments from winners scroll underneath.

steps.title: Only the postage to pay
steps.detail: Claiming costs 1.95 for shipping, by card. The small print enrols you in a monthly subscription from a merchant whose name you will not recognise.

delivery-survey-scam.whyItWorks: Companies do send feedback requests after deliveries, so the opening looks routine. By the time the prize appears you have answered questions, and that sliver of effort makes the reward feel earned instead of random.

realVsFake.real: A genuine feedback request comes from the shop or courier you used, asks for a rating and ends with thanks.
realVsFake.fake: This one ends with a prize game and a payment form, whatever answers you give.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate prize draws do not bill winners for postage before sending the prize.
realVsFake.fake: The 'free' phone needs a small shipping payment that turns into repeating charges on your statement.

realVsFake.real: Real questionnaires stay open for days and work the same whenever you answer.
realVsFake.fake: A timer gives you four minutes, and the stock counter drops each time the page reloads.

steps.title: A nudge after your order
steps.detail: A text arrives in the evening, when takeaway and grocery orders peak, saying your driver did a great job and inviting a tip.

steps.title: The driver's profile page
steps.detail: The page shows a first name, a smiling photo, a five-star rating and three buttons offering to send 2, 5 or 10.

steps.title: Card details for a gratuity
steps.detail: Picking an amount opens a form for the long card number, expiry date and security code, although the real app already holds your payment method.

steps.title: Thanks, and nothing sent
steps.detail: A cheerful confirmation appears. No driver gets a penny. The card is tested with a small charge, then used for bigger spending elsewhere.

delivery-tip-scam.whyItWorks: Tipping is a small kindness with a little guilt attached, especially if you forgot to do it at the door. A couple of coins for a named driver seems too minor to question, and the page is built around that.

realVsFake.real: Food and grocery apps take tips on the order screen inside the app, using the card you paid with.
realVsFake.fake: A texted link opens a browser page where the whole card must be typed in.

realVsFake.real: A real tip prompt names the restaurant or shop and shows the order you placed.
realVsFake.fake: The message says only 'your driver', because it was sent to thousands of numbers at once.

realVsFake.real: In genuine apps you can add a gratuity hours later, or not at all, without consequence.
realVsFake.fake: The page suggests the driver loses out unless you pay within minutes.

steps.title: A form to 'check your details'
steps.detail: A fax, letter or email asks someone at the business to confirm its name, address and phone number for a trade directory, and to sign and return it.

steps.title: The price hides in grey print
steps.detail: Near the bottom, in small type, the form states that signing places an order for a paid listing running two or three years.

steps.title: The renewal invoice lands
steps.detail: Weeks later an invoice headed 'renewal' arrives for several hundred a year, addressed to accounts payable and quoting the signed form as the contract.

steps.title: Reminders, then a 'collections' letter
steps.detail: Unpaid invoices are followed by late fees and letters from a debt collector with the same address as the directory. Many firms pay to make it stop.

directory-listing-scam.whyItWorks: The person who signs the form and the person who pays the invoice are rarely the same, so each assumes the other approved it. A directory listing is a dull, plausible expense that nobody in a busy office remembers ordering or cancelling.

realVsFake.real: A directory you actually advertise with has an order on file, a named sales contact and a listing that brings in enquiries.
realVsFake.fake: The 'directory' is a bare website few people visit, and nobody in your office recalls speaking to them.

realVsFake.real: Genuine publishers put the price and term at the top of an order form and call it an order.
realVsFake.fake: The document is styled as a free data update, with the cost and multi-year commitment tucked into a footnote.

realVsFake.real: A real renewal matches a supplier already in your accounts system, with past invoices at a similar amount.
realVsFake.fake: The word 'renewal' is used on the very first invoice, and the name echoes a well-known phone directory.

steps.title: Harvesting expiry dates
steps.detail: Scammers pull domain names, owner emails and renewal dates from public registration records and from contact pages on small business websites.

steps.title: The 'final notice' invoice
steps.detail: An email or posted letter styled as an invoice shows your domain, an expiry date and a fee several times the usual, sent by 'Domain Registry Services' or similar.

steps.title: The pay-now page
steps.detail: The link opens a card form on the sender's own site, or a copy of your registrar's login that captures the account password.

steps.title: What you actually bought
steps.detail: You have paid for nothing, or for a worthless 'search engine listing'. With the registrar login, criminals repoint your website and email and demand money to return them.

domain-renewal-scam.whyItWorks: Domains are bought once and forgotten, often by whoever built the site years ago, so few owners remember the registrar or the date. The prospect of the website and all company email going dark is enough to pay first.

realVsFake.real: Your actual registrar writes from its own domain, names your account and normally renews automatically from the card on file.
realVsFake.fake: A company you have never dealt with sends a 'final notice' as its very first contact.

realVsFake.real: Genuine renewal prices match last year's and are visible in the registrar's control panel.
realVsFake.fake: The invoice is several times higher, bundles five years or adds a 'search submission' service.

realVsFake.real: Most registrars allow a grace period after expiry during which the owner can still renew.
realVsFake.fake: The notice threatens permanent loss of the name within 24 hours.

steps.title: A letter about forgotten money
steps.detail: An email or posted letter from an 'asset reunification office' says an old savings account, pension pot or a late relative's estate has been traced to you.

steps.title: Claim form and proof of identity
steps.detail: You are asked to complete a form with your date of birth, bank account and a passport copy so the 'claims officer' can match the records.

steps.title: The release fee
steps.detail: Before payout there is a modest charge, perhaps 45 for 'administration', a 'probate stamp' or an 'unclaimed assets tax', payable by transfer.

steps.title: More hurdles, then details sold
steps.detail: Each payment produces a new obstacle: a solicitor's certificate, an anti-fraud bond. When you stop paying, your documents are used or sold for identity fraud.

dormant-account-scam.whyItWorks: Lost accounts and unclaimed estates do exist, and most people have an old savings book or a distant relative they have lost track of. A specific, modest sum of a few thousand feels more believable than a lottery jackpot.

realVsFake.real: Official lost-account tracing services are free, and you start the search yourself through the bank or a national scheme.
realVsFake.fake: Somebody you have never heard of writes to say they have already found your money.

realVsFake.real: A bank returning dormant funds asks you to prove identity, then pays the balance without deductions in advance.
realVsFake.fake: A fee must reach them before anything is released, and it cannot be taken from the balance.

realVsFake.real: Genuine heir-hunting firms can name the deceased and the family connection, and work for a share agreed in a written contract.
realVsFake.fake: The letter is vague about whose money it was and carries no postal address or company number.

steps.title: Someone shared a file with you
steps.detail: An email with the blue box logo says a named person, sometimes a real contact whose mailbox was hacked, has shared 'Invoice_0387.pdf' or 'Scan'.

steps.title: The blurred preview
steps.detail: 'View file' opens a page showing a blurred document behind a sign-in box. Some versions start on a real Dropbox page holding a PDF with a second link.

steps.title: Choose your email provider
steps.detail: The box offers Google, Microsoft 365, Yahoo or 'Other mail' and asks for your email address and its password, not a Dropbox one.

steps.title: Wrong password, try again
steps.detail: An error makes you type the password twice, then a harmless PDF loads. The attackers now read your mailbox and send the same lure to your contacts.

dropbox-shared-file-scam.whyItWorks: Shared files are how offices work, and many of these emails come from a real colleague or supplier whose account was already taken over. A blurred invoice behind a sign-in box creates enough curiosity to type a password.

realVsFake.real: A real Dropbox share opens the file in the browser, often with no sign-in, and never needs your email password.
realVsFake.fake: The page asks you to pick a mail provider and enter that password to 'view' the document.

realVsFake.real: Genuine share emails come from Dropbox's own sending address and link to its own domain.
realVsFake.fake: The button points to a form builder, a file host or a domain registered last week.

realVsFake.real: A colleague sharing something usually mentions it first, and the file name relates to work you know about.
realVsFake.fake: There is no covering note, a generic file name and a line about access expiring.

steps.title: The quota warning
steps.detail: An email from 'Mail Administrator' or 'IT Helpdesk' shows a red bar nearly at its limit and says incoming messages are being held back.

steps.title: Release pending messages
steps.detail: Buttons offer a free storage upgrade or the release of 'seven held messages', with a note that queued mail will be deleted after 48 hours.

steps.title: A login that already knows you
steps.detail: The page shows your email address pre-filled and your provider's or employer's logo pulled in automatically, leaving only the password box empty.

steps.title: The mailbox becomes a master key
steps.detail: With mailbox access, the criminals add a forwarding rule, search for invoices and bank messages, reset passwords on other accounts and send phishing from your address.

email-storage-full-scam.whyItWorks: Mailboxes do fill up and real providers do send quota warnings, so the message matches something people have seen before. Finding your own address already typed into the form feels like proof that the page knows you.

realVsFake.real: Your provider shows storage use inside mailbox settings, and a truly full mailbox bounces mail back to the sender.
realVsFake.fake: The email claims messages are queued somewhere and will be wiped unless you sign in.

realVsFake.real: A workplace IT team writes from an internal address, signs with a name and can be phoned.
realVsFake.fake: The sender is 'Admin Team' at an outside domain, with no name and no extension number.

realVsFake.real: Extra storage is bought or freed from your account's own subscription page.
realVsFake.fake: The 'upgrade' is free, instant and needs nothing except your password.

steps.title: A mailbox is broken into first
steps.detail: Long before you see anything, someone in the conversation loses their email password to an earlier phish. The intruder reads their sent folder and picks threads still in progress.

steps.title: A reply lands mid-conversation
steps.detail: A new message arrives under the subject line you know, 'Re: Project update', with every earlier email quoted below it. The only new part is one short line and a file.

steps.title: The document wants a login
steps.detail: The link opens a page styled like a shared-drive viewer and asks for your email password to show the 'revised document', or the attachment asks you to enable content.

steps.title: Your contacts get the next reply
steps.detail: With your password or a foothold on your machine, the intruder searches your own inbox for live threads and sends the same one-line reply to the people you were writing to.

email-thread-hijacking-scam.whyItWorks: You check a stranger's email carefully, but a reply sitting under your own words from last Tuesday gets none of that scrutiny. The quoted history is real, so the one invented line borrows all of its credibility.

realVsFake.real: A colleague sending a revised file usually says what changed and refers to something specific from the earlier discussion.
realVsFake.fake: The hijacked reply is one generic line, 'please see attached and let me know your thoughts', that would fit under any thread at all.

realVsFake.real: Files from a real contact open in the tool your team already uses, without asking for your mailbox password again.
realVsFake.fake: The link leads to an unfamiliar viewer page that wants your email address and password before it will show anything.

realVsFake.real: Your contact will confirm they sent it if you ring them or message them on a different app.
realVsFake.fake: A reply to the email itself reaches the intruder, who answers 'yes, that was me' and urges you to open it.

steps.title: An order you never placed
steps.detail: An email styled like an Amazon confirmation thanks you for buying a laptop at 1,299.99, with a delivery address in another city and an order number that looks plausible.

steps.title: The cancel button and helpline
steps.detail: Underneath sit a 'Cancel order' button and a support phone number. Both occupy the spot where the genuine email would put 'View or manage order'.

steps.title: Sign in to stop the delivery
steps.detail: The button opens a copy of the Amazon sign-in screen. After your password it asks you to 'confirm the card on file', security code included, to process the cancellation.

steps.title: A refunds agent on the phone
steps.detail: People who ring the number reach a 'refunds agent' who asks for the one-time passcode Amazon just texted, or for gift cards to 'reverse' the charge.

fake-amazon-order-email.whyItWorks: Seeing a four-figure purchase headed to a stranger's address makes you think your account has already been broken into. Cancelling feels like the careful thing to do, and the email has put the button right there.

realVsFake.real: Every genuine order appears under Your Orders when you open the Amazon app or type the site address yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The laptop exists only in the email. Nothing matching it shows in your order history or on your card statement.

realVsFake.real: Amazon lets you cancel an unshipped item from the order page, with no need to re-enter a card number.
realVsFake.fake: The cancellation page asks for the full card number, expiry date and security code before it will 'stop the shipment'.

realVsFake.real: Amazon does not ask customers to pay for or verify anything with gift cards, and its staff never need your sign-in passcode.
realVsFake.fake: The agent on the support line says gift cards are how the refund is 'balanced', and wants the codes read aloud.

steps.title: Locked for your security
steps.detail: Under an Apple logo, the email says your Apple ID was locked after a sign-in attempt from another country. You have 24 hours to verify or the account is disabled.

steps.title: A sign-in page on another address
steps.detail: The 'Unlock account' button opens a white page with the Apple logo and two boxes. The address bar shows a long string with 'apple' buried somewhere in the middle.

steps.title: Identity questions pile up
steps.detail: After the password, further screens ask for your date of birth, the answers to your security questions and sometimes a card 'to confirm ownership of the account'.

steps.title: The six-digit code
steps.detail: As the criminal signs in with what you typed, your iPhone shows a real verification code. The fake page has a box waiting for it, and entering it hands over the account.

fake-apple-id-locked-email.whyItWorks: An Apple ID sits behind your photos, messages and every device you own, so the word 'locked' lands hard. Apple does lock accounts for security reasons, which makes the story plausible before you have looked at the link.

realVsFake.real: When an Apple ID really is locked, your own iPhone or Mac says so on screen the next time you use it.
realVsFake.fake: The only sign of a lock is the email. Your devices carry on working normally, and so does the App Store.

realVsFake.real: Apple unlocks accounts through its own recovery process, started from your device settings or by typing Apple's account address yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The email supplies its own button and says the unlock must happen through that link within the day.

realVsFake.real: Apple staff never ask you to share a verification code, and the prompt on your device shows roughly where the sign-in is coming from.
realVsFake.fake: The page asks for the code that just appeared on your phone and calls it 'the final step to unlock'.

steps.title: An 'update required' text
steps.detail: A message or search advert says your bank's app is being retired, with a button to install the replacement. On Android it downloads a file ending in .apk.

steps.title: Switching off the phone's defences
steps.detail: The installer asks you to allow 'unknown sources', then to grant accessibility permission, which lets the app read the screen and press buttons by itself.

steps.title: A login screen that matches
steps.detail: It opens with the bank's logo and colours. You type customer number, password and card details, which are sent straight to the operator.

steps.title: Texts read silently
steps.detail: With permission to read messages, the malware forwards one-time codes unseen, or draws a fake 'updating' screen over the real app while money is moved.

fake-banking-app-scam.whyItWorks: Apps demand updates constantly, so one more prompt looks routine, and a warning that access is about to stop gives a practical reason to act now. On a small screen, a copied logo is all most people check.

realVsFake.real: A bank's app updates through the phone's official store, usually automatically, with no action needed.
realVsFake.fake: You are sent a download link by text or email and told the store version no longer works.

realVsFake.real: The genuine app is listed under the bank's registered name with a long history of reviews.
realVsFake.fake: The fake has a publisher name like 'Secure Mobile Ltd', a handful of five-star reviews and a release date last week.

realVsFake.real: Real banking apps ask for a passcode or fingerprint on opening, using details you set up before.
realVsFake.fake: The counterfeit asks for everything at once on first launch: full password, card number, CVV and telephone banking PIN.

steps.title: A buyer, a job or a prize
steps.detail: Someone answers your online advert without haggling, hires you as a 'mystery shopper' or 'personal assistant', or announces a sweepstake win. Payment will come by cheque.

steps.title: The envelope arrives
steps.detail: A professional-looking cheque or banker's draft turns up by courier, drawn on a real company's account, for noticeably more than agreed.

steps.title: Funds 'available' the next day
steps.detail: You pay it in and the balance rises, because banks often release money before a cheque has been fully checked. The sender calls this proof it cleared.

steps.title: Send back the surplus
steps.detail: They ask you to forward the excess to a 'shipping agent' or 'supplier' by wire, payment app or gift cards. Later the cheque is returned as forged.

fake-cheque-scam.whyItWorks: Most people believe that once money shows in their balance, the cheque is good. In fact the bank has only advanced the funds, and discovering a forgery can take weeks, long after the difference has been sent on.

realVsFake.real: A genuine buyer pays the asking price, and one who overpays by mistake can cancel the cheque and write a correct one.
realVsFake.fake: The sender wants you to bank the oversized cheque and return the surplus yourself, today.

realVsFake.real: Employers pay wages after you have worked and do not route company money through a new starter's account.
realVsFake.fake: Your first 'task' is to deposit a cheque and buy gift cards or wire funds with it.

realVsFake.real: Lotteries and competitions pay winnings in full without asking for anything back.
realVsFake.fake: The 'prize' cheque comes with instructions to return part of it for taxes or handling.

steps.title: A new friend mentions an exchange
steps.detail: Someone met on a dating app or through a 'wrong number' text chats for weeks, then mentions an uncle or analyst who gives them trading tips on a particular exchange.

steps.title: An app from outside the store
steps.detail: They send a link to the exchange's website or an app installed through a test-build link. It has live price charts and a customer service chat.

steps.title: Buy real coins, send them across
steps.detail: You buy crypto on a well-known exchange and transfer it to a deposit address on the fake one. Guided trades show profit, and one small withdrawal succeeds.

steps.title: The tax bill on 8,400
steps.detail: When you try to cash out the 8,400 shown, support demands a tax payment sent to a wallet first, then a security deposit, then freezes the account for 'money laundering'.

fake-crypto-exchange-scam.whyItWorks: The first purchase happens on a genuine exchange, so everything feels legitimate up to the moment coins are sent across. The balance on the fake site is only a number typed into a database, but it looks like winnings worth paying a fee to collect.

realVsFake.real: Established exchanges are installed from the official app stores and have years of public history under one name.
realVsFake.fake: The app comes through a direct download or beta-testing link, and the web address changes every few weeks.

realVsFake.real: An exchange takes trading and withdrawal fees out of your balance. Tax is a matter between you and your own tax authority.
realVsFake.fake: Support insists the tax cannot be deducted from the profit and must arrive as a separate deposit within 48 hours.

realVsFake.real: Regulated platforms verify your identity before you fund the account, during sign-up.
realVsFake.fake: Deposits are accepted with no checks at all, and 'verification' is raised for the first time when you ask for money out.

steps.title: An advert above the real result
steps.detail: Searching for a wallet by name brings up a sponsored link first, or an app store shows a clone with a near-identical icon and a slightly different developer.

steps.title: Installed and looking right
steps.detail: The app or browser extension opens with the familiar fox, shield or colour scheme. Its welcome screen offers 'Create new wallet' or 'Import existing wallet'.

steps.title: Twelve words typed in
steps.detail: Choosing import, you type your 12-word recovery phrase to restore the wallet. Some clones instead show an error and ask you to 'verify' the phrase again.

steps.title: Restored on the thief's device
steps.detail: The phrase is transmitted to the criminals, who restore your wallet on their own machine and send every coin out. With clones that generate a new wallet, they already hold its phrase.

fake-crypto-wallet-scam.whyItWorks: Entering a recovery phrase is exactly what a genuine wallet asks for when you move to a new phone, so the request raises no alarm. The fraud lies entirely in which program is asking, and adverts and store listings make that hard to judge.

realVsFake.real: Wallet makers link to their downloads from their own website, and the store listing shows the same developer name.
realVsFake.fake: The listing has a publisher name with an extra word or character, a recent release date and a handful of five-star reviews.

realVsFake.real: A genuine wallet asks for your phrase once, on your own decision to restore, and never through a pop-up or email.
realVsFake.fake: A warning says the wallet will be locked unless you re-enter the phrase to verify your account.

realVsFake.real: Hardware wallets show the phrase on the device's own screen at set-up and ask you to write it down.
realVsFake.fake: A companion app or a card in the box tells you to type the words into a phone or computer.

steps.title: A voicemail from 'legal processing'
steps.detail: A recorded or live message gives a 'case number' and says papers will be served at your home or workplace unless you ring back today.

steps.title: Details that sound right
steps.detail: The collector recites part of your national insurance or social security number, an old address, or the name of a payday lender you once used.

steps.title: The threat ladder
steps.detail: They say officers are on the way, your employer will be informed, your licence suspended. Then comes a 'one-time settlement' at half the balance, valid for this call.

steps.title: Payment over the phone
steps.detail: A debit card number is taken, or you are directed to a transfer, payment app or prepaid card. No receipt or settlement letter ever arrives, and the calls return.

fake-debt-collector-scam.whyItWorks: Plenty of people have an old overdraft, payday loan or phone bill they are not sure was ever settled, so the claim cannot be dismissed outright. Talk of arrest or a visit to the workplace adds shame, which stops people asking family for advice.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate collection agency sends a written notice naming the original creditor, the amount, and how to dispute it.
realVsFake.fake: The caller says there is no time for letters and that asking for proof is 'refusal to cooperate'.

realVsFake.real: Unpaid consumer debt is a civil matter. Collectors cannot have you arrested, and court papers come from a court.
realVsFake.fake: A 'warrant' or 'sheriff visit' is promised for this afternoon unless a card payment is made now.

realVsFake.real: Proper agencies accept traceable payment into a company account and confirm it in writing.
realVsFake.fake: You are given a personal account, a prepaid card reload or a payment-app handle to send the money to.

steps.title: A document awaits your signature
steps.detail: An email laid out like a DocuSign notice, yellow button included, says a company you have never dealt with sent 'Contract_Final.pdf' for signature and that the envelope expires soon.

steps.title: Review Document goes elsewhere
steps.detail: 'Review Document' does not open a signing screen. It lands on a page offering to 'continue with Outlook, Gmail or Office 365' so the file can be 'securely decrypted'.

steps.title: A password in place of a signature
steps.detail: You pick your provider and type your mailbox password into a copied login box. The page then shows an error or a blank PDF, with nothing to sign.

steps.title: The mailbox is the prize
steps.detail: With the password, the criminal reads your inbox for invoices and contracts in progress, sets a forwarding rule, and sends the same fake envelope to your contacts.

fake-docusign-email-scam.whyItWorks: Signing requests routinely arrive from senders you have never heard of: a letting agent's system, a new supplier, a solicitor's office. An unfamiliar name on a DocuSign notice does not feel odd, and 'expires soon' discourages asking around first.

realVsFake.real: A genuine DocuSign notice carries a security code you can enter on the DocuSign site yourself to open the envelope without clicking anything.
realVsFake.fake: The fake has no code, or one that leads nowhere. Its button is the only route offered to the document.

realVsFake.real: Signing a real envelope needs no password for your mailbox. You open the document and add your signature.
realVsFake.fake: Before any document appears, a box asks for your email account password 'to verify the recipient'.

realVsFake.real: Whoever sent a real contract can tell you what it is when you ask them directly.
realVsFake.fake: The sender is a vague 'Accounts Department' or a firm with no reason to send you paperwork.

steps.title: One new message from a recruiter
steps.detail: The email uses LinkedIn's blue header and says a recruiter messaged you about a role, or that you 'appeared in 9 searches this week'. A button says 'View message'.

steps.title: A login screen on the wrong address
steps.detail: That button brings up a replica of the LinkedIn login screen hosted somewhere else. Typing your email and password there sends both to whoever runs the page.

steps.title: The recruiter moves to WhatsApp
steps.detail: In the job-offer version a friendly hiring manager replies, praises your profile, and asks to move to WhatsApp or Telegram for a 'quick text interview'.

steps.title: Fees, forms and a borrowed profile
steps.detail: You are offered the job within days, then asked for passport scans, bank details 'for payroll' or a fee for training or equipment. Meanwhile your stolen login messages your connections.

fake-linkedin-email-scam.whyItWorks: LinkedIn sends so many notification emails that clicking through is a habit, and a message from a recruiter is exactly what the site exists for. Anyone job hunting wants this particular email to be real.

realVsFake.real: Real LinkedIn messages are waiting in the Messaging tab when you open the app yourself.
realVsFake.fake: Open the app and no recruiter has written to you. The promised message is nowhere in your Messaging tab.

realVsFake.real: A real recruiter names the employer and the role, and is content to hold a proper interview by video or phone.
realVsFake.fake: The hiring manager avoids calls, interviews by text chat only, and offers the job after a handful of questions.

realVsFake.real: Employers pay you. Equipment and training are provided, or reimbursed through payroll once you have started.
realVsFake.fake: Before any start date you are asked to pay for a laptop, a background check or a training pack.

steps.title: 'We're having trouble with your billing'
steps.detail: A red-and-black email says Netflix could not take this month's payment and your account is on hold. It gives you 24 hours before the membership is cancelled.

steps.title: The red 'Update account' button
steps.detail: It leads to a dark sign-in screen identical to the real one, on an address that merely contains the brand's name. You type your email and password as usual.

steps.title: A billing form with extras
steps.detail: The next page asks for the card number, expiry, security code and billing postcode. Some versions add your date of birth, which a streaming service has no use for.

steps.title: A code from your bank
steps.detail: A final screen says your bank must verify the card and asks for the code it just texted. That code approves a purchase the criminal is making elsewhere.

fake-netflix-payment-email.whyItWorks: A Netflix login is often shared across a household, so whoever opens the email assumes someone else's card has expired and does not want to be the reason the television goes dark tonight. Failed payments are common enough that nothing sounds odd.

realVsFake.real: When a Netflix payment really fails, the app or the TV shows a notice the next time someone tries to watch.
realVsFake.fake: Netflix still plays normally on your television while the email insists the account is on hold.

realVsFake.real: Netflix does not ask for card numbers or passwords to be sent by email or text. Billing is changed under Account after you sign in yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The email takes you straight to a card form through its own link and never mentions the Account page.

realVsFake.real: A real billing hold simply pauses playback until a working card is added. There is no countdown.
realVsFake.fake: You get 24 hours, a ticking timer, and a threat that your profiles and viewing history will be erased.

steps.title: Your account has been limited
steps.detail: PayPal has supposedly noticed unusual activity and restricted sending and withdrawing until you confirm your information. The message opens with 'Dear Customer' and ends with a 'Resolve now' button.

steps.title: A cloned login screen
steps.detail: The button leads to a page with the PayPal logo and the familiar two-box login. The address is a lookalike, often 'paypal' followed by extra words and hyphens.

steps.title: The 'confirm your identity' form
steps.detail: Once the password is in, a second form asks for your full name, address, card number, and the bank account linked to your PayPal balance.

steps.title: Balance sent as friends and family
steps.detail: The criminal logs in, changes the email and phone on the account, and sends the balance to another account as a personal payment, which carries no buyer protection.

fake-paypal-email-scam.whyItWorks: PayPal really does limit accounts, and sellers in particular dread it because their money gets frozen. The scam borrows the genuine term 'limited', so anyone who has heard of a real limitation assumes this is one.

realVsFake.real: PayPal emails address you by the full name on your account, or by your business name.
realVsFake.fake: The greeting is 'Dear Customer', 'Dear User' or just your email address pasted in.

realVsFake.real: A real limitation is listed in the Resolution Centre when you log in by typing the address yourself, with the steps needed to lift it.
realVsFake.fake: Log in the normal way and no limitation is listed. The restriction lives only on the page behind the emailed button.

realVsFake.real: PayPal does not ask for your password, full card number or bank details by email.
realVsFake.fake: The form wants all three on one page and says access stays frozen until every box is filled.

steps.title: A quote request from 'procurement'
steps.detail: An email signed by a named purchasing officer at a university or large company asks for prices on laptops, hard drives, projectors or lab equipment.

steps.title: The purchase order PDF
steps.detail: Your quote is accepted without negotiation. A purchase order follows with the institution's logo, a PO number and a request for standard 30-day credit terms.

steps.title: Deliver to a different address
steps.detail: The ship-to line is a warehouse, self-storage unit or residential address described as an off-campus receiving site, where a freight forwarder re-ships the goods.

steps.title: The invoice reaches the real organisation
steps.detail: After thirty days you chase payment. The genuine accounts office has no record of the order, the officer never wrote to you, and the stock is long gone.

fake-purchase-order-scam.whyItWorks: Universities and public bodies are known to pay reliably on credit, and landing one as a customer feels like a break for a small supplier. The officer's name is real and can be found on the institution's website, which passes a quick check.

realVsFake.real: A genuine institution emails from its own domain and asks new suppliers to complete vendor registration before ordering.
realVsFake.fake: The address swaps a letter, adds a hyphen or ends in a different suffix, and no supplier onboarding is mentioned.

realVsFake.real: Real orders deliver to the organisation's own campus, depot or office, through its goods-in department.
realVsFake.fake: The delivery address is in another town, and the contact asks for the tracking number the moment the goods leave.

realVsFake.real: Purchasing staff can be reached through the main switchboard listed on the official website.
realVsFake.fake: The only phone number is the one on the purchase order, answered by a mobile or an internet voice line.

steps.title: The screen that will not close
steps.detail: A browser tab goes full screen with a Microsoft logo, a count of 'viruses found', a looping alarm sound and a line saying 'Do not restart. Call support.'

steps.title: The diagnosis on the phone
steps.detail: The 'engineer' who answers gives a badge number, asks you to press Windows and R, and has you type a command that fills the screen with harmless listings he calls infections.

steps.title: A tool that hands over control
steps.detail: Next comes a legitimate remote-control program such as AnyDesk or TeamViewer. You install it and read out the number it displays, which lets him move your mouse and open your files.

steps.title: The lifetime protection plan
steps.detail: He quotes a one-off fee or a 'lifetime protection plan' of a few hundred, payable by card over the phone or by gift cards. Some then set a password that locks you out.

fake-tech-support-scam.whyItWorks: The page is built to look as if the computer itself is speaking: it hides the browser's edges and refuses to close. A frozen screen and a blaring alarm leave the printed phone number as the only obvious way out.

realVsFake.real: Microsoft says its error messages never include a phone number, and it does not ring customers about viruses.
realVsFake.fake: A toll-free number sits in the middle of the alert, sometimes read aloud by a recorded voice.

realVsFake.real: A genuine security warning comes from the antivirus program installed on your machine and can be dismissed like any other window.
realVsFake.fake: The alert lives in a browser tab, blocks the close button, and says restarting will destroy your data.

realVsFake.real: A repair shop quotes a price before starting work, on a job you brought to them.
realVsFake.fake: The price appears only after he controls the screen, and gift cards are suggested as the fastest way to pay.

steps.title: Invited to a VIP signals group
steps.detail: You are added to a messaging channel where an admin posts currency pair tips and members reply with screenshots of winning trades and thanks.

steps.title: Let me manage it for you
steps.detail: The admin messages privately, offering to trade your account for a share of profit. You are told to open one with a broker he names and fund it.

steps.title: Up sixty in a month
steps.detail: The broker's dashboard shows fast growth. He says a major trade on the pound or gold is coming and you need a bigger balance to qualify, perhaps with a deposit bonus.

steps.title: Margin call or missing manager
steps.detail: When you ask to withdraw, the bonus terms require impossible trading volume, or a sudden losing position needs topping up. Soon after, the manager and broker stop replying.

forex-trading-scam.whyItWorks: Currency trading is a real profession full of jargon about pips, lots and margin, so handing the decisions to a confident manager seems sensible. The group's daily stream of other members' wins makes staying out feel like the costly choice.

realVsFake.real: A licensed forex broker appears on the financial regulator's register and carries a prominent warning about the risk of losses.
realVsFake.fake: The broker is registered on a small island or nowhere, and its site talks only about winning months.

realVsFake.real: Anyone managing money for others needs authorisation and works under a written agreement with their firm's name on it.
realVsFake.fake: The 'account manager' is a first name and a profile photo, and asks for your trading password or remote access.

realVsFake.real: Withdrawals from a genuine broker return to the bank account or card that funded it, usually within days.
realVsFake.fake: Deposits are requested in crypto or to rotating personal accounts, and cashing out triggers a 'verification' charge.

steps.title: A client has hired you
steps.detail: The email copies the styling of a site such as Upwork or Fiverr and says a client accepted your proposal. A button reads 'Accept contract', above a brief of two vague lines.

steps.title: Log in, or message on WhatsApp
steps.detail: The button leads to a fake platform sign-in that takes your password. Alternatively the 'client' gives a WhatsApp number and says the site's own chat is 'too slow'.

steps.title: Payment outside the platform
steps.detail: Off-platform, they offer to pay by cheque or bank transfer 'to save you the service fee', then send more than agreed or ask for a refundable 'onboarding deposit' first.

steps.title: Send back the difference
steps.detail: You are asked to return the overpaid amount, or forward it to their 'designer', before the cheque bounces or the transfer is reversed. The work itself is never paid for.

freelance-platform-email-scam.whyItWorks: Freelancers send out dozens of proposals and wait, so an email saying one has landed is the best news of the week. Platform fees are a real irritation, which makes a client's offer to skip them sound generous.

realVsFake.real: Real offers and contracts sit in your dashboard on the platform, where you accept them after logging in the usual way.
realVsFake.fake: Your dashboard shows no new contract and no message from that client. The offer is nowhere but the inbox.

realVsFake.real: Platforms hold a client's money in escrow or charge it up front, then release it to you through the site.
realVsFake.fake: The client proposes a cheque, a direct transfer or a payment app, and wants your bank details in chat.

realVsFake.real: A genuine client pays what was agreed and has no reason to send extra.
realVsFake.fake: An overpayment arrives 'by mistake', followed by a polite, pressing request to wire the surplus to a third person.

steps.title: Found through your own complaint
steps.detail: After you post about your loss on a forum or review site, or because your name is on a list sold by the original fraudsters, a 'recovery specialist' gets in touch.

steps.title: They have 'traced' your money
steps.detail: They claim blockchain analysis or an international task force has located the funds in a frozen wallet or overseas account, and email an impressive report with seals.

steps.title: The retainer
steps.detail: To begin, they need a legal retainer, a 'court filing cost' or a refundable deposit, usually requested in crypto or by wire to a foreign account.

steps.title: The wallet 'sync'
steps.detail: Next they ask for your exchange login or seed phrase to 'return the coins', or for banking details to 'receive the refund'. Whatever is left gets taken.

fund-recovery-scam.whyItWorks: After a loss, the hope of undoing it is stronger than caution, and the caller names the exact platform and amount involved. An official-sounding title such as 'asset recovery division' suggests that somebody in authority is finally on your side.

realVsFake.real: Police, regulators and your bank's fraud department do not charge victims to investigate or return money.
realVsFake.fake: A private 'agency' wants a fee, tax or deposit paid before it will lift a finger.

realVsFake.real: A genuine solicitor can be looked up on the professional regulator's register and will not promise a result.
realVsFake.fake: The 'lawyer' guarantees full recovery within days and has a website registered only recently.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate investigators never need the recovery phrase for your crypto wallet or your online banking password.
realVsFake.fake: They say the refund must be 'synchronised' with your wallet and ask for the twelve words.

steps.title: A 100k account for a small fee
steps.detail: An advert offers the chance to trade the firm's capital and keep most of the profit. All you pay is a challenge fee of a few hundred.

steps.title: The evaluation rules
steps.detail: You get a demo login with a profit target, a daily loss limit and a time limit. Extra rules about news events, lot sizes and 'consistency' sit deep in the terms.

steps.title: Breached, with a reset on offer
steps.detail: A widened spread or slipped stop-loss tips the account past the daily limit. An email declares the challenge failed and offers a discounted reset if bought within a day.

steps.title: Passing brings a payout review
steps.detail: Traders who do pass and request a payout are told a rule was broken in hindsight, and the account is closed. Others find the firm's site and chat server gone.

funded-trader-scam.whyItWorks: The offer flatters a trader's belief that only a lack of capital is holding them back. Each failure looks like their own mistake, so buying another attempt feels like persistence, and the firm earns from fees whether anyone is ever funded.

realVsFake.real: A credible prop firm publishes every rule before you pay and applies the same rules after you pass.
realVsFake.fake: New conditions surface at payout time, citing clauses such as 'abusive trading' that are never defined.

realVsFake.real: Firms that do pay can show a long record of withdrawals confirmed by traders on independent forums.
realVsFake.fake: Proof of payouts is a wall of certificate images on the firm's own site, and its company registration is weeks old.

realVsFake.real: An honest evaluation uses price feeds that match the wider market, so results can be checked against another platform.
realVsFake.fake: Prices on the firm's in-house platform spike in ways no other chart shows, always at the moment a limit is near.

steps.title: A maxed account, priced to go
steps.detail: In a Discord server, marketplace group or forum, a seller posts screenshots of a high-level account with rare skins at well under the going rate: 'quitting the game, need it gone today'.

steps.title: Friends and family only
steps.detail: In direct messages the seller wants PayPal friends and family, crypto or a gift card code, and refuses the group's middleman 'because the last one robbed me'.

steps.title: The login arrives and works
steps.detail: After payment you receive an email and password that work. You log in, change the password, and for a few days the account appears to be yours.

steps.title: Pulled back by the original owner
steps.detail: The seller contacts the game's support with the original receipts and creation email, has the account 'recovered', and resells it. Support will not help you, because buying accounts breaks the terms.

game-account-trading-scam.whyItWorks: Hundreds of hours of grinding or a discontinued skin cannot be bought from the publisher at any price, so the grey market is the only source. Buyers already know they are breaking the rules, which makes them slower to ask questions or complain.

realVsFake.real: Where a game allows trading at all, it happens through an in-game trade window or official marketplace that swaps both sides at once.
realVsFake.fake: The deal runs on trust in a chat window: you send money first and wait for a login to appear.

realVsFake.real: Whoever created an account keeps the proof of ownership for good: the first email address and the earliest receipts.
realVsFake.fake: The seller promises 'full access, original email included' but can still reclaim everything through support months later.

realVsFake.real: A payment for goods carries some protection, and an honest seller accepts that.
realVsFake.fake: Only irreversible payment is accepted. As a buyer, the same scammer pays, takes your account, then files a chargeback.

steps.title: An invite from a 'developer'
steps.detail: A Discord message, often from a friend's hacked account, says 'we're testing our new game, want to try it and give feedback?' and links to a polished site with a trailer.

steps.title: The launcher download
steps.detail: The site offers a 'beta client' installer inside a password-protected archive, with the access key shown beside the button. The password also stops email and browser scanners looking inside.

steps.title: It crashes on launch
steps.detail: You run the installer and get an error such as 'missing DLL', or a window that closes. The 'developer' apologises and stops replying. The real work has already been done.

steps.title: Sessions and wallets drained
steps.detail: An info-stealer has copied your browser's saved logins, Discord and Steam session tokens and any crypto wallet files. Your Discord account then sends the same invite to your friends.

game-beta-scam.whyItWorks: Closed betas for anticipated games really are handed out through invites and keys, and getting one feels like luck. When the message comes from a friend's account, asking for a favour, the request is flattering and hard to refuse.

realVsFake.real: Real betas are distributed through Steam playtests, console stores or the publisher's own launcher, after you sign up on the official site.
realVsFake.fake: The 'client' comes from a file-sharing link or a brand-new website and is unknown to any store.

realVsFake.real: A real studio has a history: earlier games, named staff, store pages and a social account older than a few weeks.
realVsFake.fake: The studio's site was registered recently, the trailer is borrowed from another game, and the team cannot be found anywhere.

realVsFake.real: A game tester is never asked to switch off antivirus or connect a crypto wallet to start playing.
realVsFake.fake: The instructions say to 'disable your antivirus, it gives a false positive' and to link a wallet for 'tester rewards'.

steps.title: Guaranteed rank in three days
steps.detail: An advert in a game's Discord, a comment under a ranked video or a slick website promises a climb to the top tier, with a price list by division and 'pro players on standby'.

steps.title: Pay first, then share the login
steps.detail: You pay up front, usually by crypto or a friends-and-family transfer, and are told to send your username and password and switch off two-step login 'so the booster can get in'.

steps.title: A few wins for show
steps.detail: Some services play a handful of matches so the rank ticks up. Then comes a request for a top-up: the account is 'harder than quoted' or needs a 'priority slot'.

steps.title: Stripped or held hostage
steps.detail: The booster changes the email and password, trades away skins and currency, and sells the account. Others demand a ransom to return it, or simply stop logging in once paid.

game-boosting-scam.whyItWorks: Being stuck one division below your friends is a specific, nagging frustration, and boosting is an open secret in ranked games, so the service itself sounds normal. Handing over the password seems unavoidable because someone else has to play.

realVsFake.real: Most publishers treat account sharing and paid boosting as a breach of their rules, and punish the account owner with rank resets or bans.
realVsFake.fake: The site calls its boosting 'safe and undetectable' and offers a ban-proof guarantee it has no way to honour.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate coaching happens with you at the controls: a stronger player reviews your matches or plays alongside in a party.
realVsFake.fake: The service insists on your password, and on two-step protection being switched off, before work begins.

realVsFake.real: A real business has traceable reviews away from its own website and takes payment methods that allow a dispute.
realVsFake.fake: Testimonials exist only as screenshots on the seller's page, and payment must be crypto or a gift code.

steps.title: Unlimited coins, no download
steps.detail: A short video or search result shows someone typing a username into a site and watching the balance jump. The link in the description leads to the 'generator'.

steps.title: Username, platform, amount
steps.detail: The page asks for your in-game name, your platform and how much currency you want, then plays a fake console animation: 'Connecting to server... injecting 10,000 coins.'

steps.title: Human verification
steps.detail: At the last moment a box says you must prove you are not a bot by completing two 'offers': a quiz, a mobile game install, a prize draw needing a phone number.

steps.title: Paid per click, plus your details
steps.detail: Each offer earns the site owner a commission. Phone numbers get signed up to premium-rate texts, and some versions ask for the account password, which is then used to empty it.

game-currency-generator-scam.whyItWorks: The audience is mostly children and teenagers who cannot buy currency without asking a parent. The animation, with its scrolling code and rising counter, looks like hacking does in films, and the comments underneath are full of invented success stories.

realVsFake.real: In-game currency is stored on the publisher's servers and is added only by buying it in the official store or earning it in play.
realVsFake.fake: A third-party web page claims it can add coins to any account from outside with just a username.

realVsFake.real: Official giveaways are announced on the game's verified channels and delivered as redeemable codes.
realVsFake.fake: The offer comes from an anonymous video with comments switched off or filled with identical praise.

realVsFake.real: A real CAPTCHA is a quick puzzle on the same page that takes seconds.
realVsFake.fake: 'Verification' means installing apps and entering a mobile number on other sites, and it never completes however many you finish.

steps.title: A renewal you never agreed to
steps.detail: You are thanked for renewing 'Geek Squad Protection' for another year at 399.99. An invoice number is quoted, and the charge will supposedly reach your statement within a day.

steps.title: One way to cancel: the phone
steps.detail: There is no link, only a toll-free number. The message often comes from a free webmail address with the invoice as an image or PDF, which helps it slip past spam filters.

steps.title: The refund form
steps.detail: The agent agrees to refund you, has you install a remote-access tool 'to open the cancellation form', then asks you to log in to your bank and type the amount yourself.

steps.title: Too many zeros
steps.detail: The screen blanks briefly. He then shows a bank balance edited to suggest 3,999 was refunded instead of 399, pleads for his job, and asks for the difference back by wire or gift cards.

geek-squad-renewal-email-scam.whyItWorks: The email asks for nothing, which is what disarms people. You make the call yourself, to cancel a charge and get money back, so by the time the agent mentions remote access you believe you are talking to a billing department.

realVsFake.real: Geek Squad plans are sold through Best Buy, and any plan you hold can be checked in your Best Buy account or in store.
realVsFake.fake: The invoice names no card, no store and no account of yours. The 'customer ID' is a random string.

realVsFake.real: A real refund is sent back to the original payment card by the retailer. You take no part in processing it.
realVsFake.fake: The agent says you must enter the refund amount yourself while he watches your banking screen.

realVsFake.real: If a business refunds too much, it corrects the mistake through the card network or the bank.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to drive to a shop, buy gift cards for the 'extra' amount, and stay on the line throughout.

steps.title: A call about protecting savings
steps.detail: A salesperson rings, or an advert follows your searches, warning that inflation and shaky banks are about to eat your savings and that physical gold is the shelter.

steps.title: The senior metals broker
steps.detail: A named account manager phones most days and posts a brochure. He quotes 'collector grade' coins and bars at a price far above the daily bullion rate.

steps.title: Vault storage instead of delivery
steps.detail: Home delivery is discouraged as unsafe. Your metal will sit in their 'allocated vault', and you receive a certificate with a bar number in place of anything you can hold.

steps.title: The bars you cannot collect
steps.detail: You wire savings or move a retirement account. Asking later to sell or collect brings storage arrears, a buy-back delay, and then a dead phone line.

gold-investment-scam.whyItWorks: Gold feels like the opposite of a gamble, a solid thing that grandparents trusted. A salesperson talking about fear of banks is repeating what the buyer already believes, so nobody asks to see the metal.

realVsFake.real: A reputable bullion dealer publishes buy and sell prices beside the live market rate, so you can compare before ordering.
realVsFake.fake: The price arrives only by phone, wrapped in a 'portfolio' of coins whose mark-up is never stated.

realVsFake.real: Genuine storage is with a named independent vault that issues its own bar list and lets you take delivery.
realVsFake.fake: Storage is 'in our secure facility', proven by a certificate the firm printed itself, and delivery requests trigger new fees.

realVsFake.real: Honest dealers say plainly that gold pays no income and its price can fall for years.
realVsFake.fake: The pitch promises a fixed yearly return on your gold and a deadline before prices 'jump next week'.

steps.title: Your listing is pending removal
steps.detail: Styled in Google's colours, the warning says your Business Profile failed a verification check and will disappear from Search and Maps in 48 hours unless you confirm ownership.

steps.title: The 'verify listing' page
steps.detail: The link opens a form showing your shop's name and address, copied from the public listing. It asks you to sign in with the Google account that manages the profile.

steps.title: A fee to stay visible
steps.detail: Some versions add a payment page: an annual 'listing maintenance' or 'verification' charge, often under a hundred, to be paid by card before the deadline.

steps.title: The profile changes hands
steps.detail: With the login, the criminal adds himself as an owner, removes you, and can swap the phone number on the listing for his own or demand money to hand it back.

google-business-email-scam.whyItWorks: For a café, plumber or salon, the map listing is where most new customers come from, so losing it sounds like losing the business. Owners also know Google does ask for verification, though few remember exactly how it was done.

realVsFake.real: Appearing on Google Search and Maps is free. Google does not charge to create, verify or keep a Business Profile.
realVsFake.fake: The email quotes a yearly fee to keep the listing live and warns that non-payment means removal.

realVsFake.real: A real suspension shows as a status on the profile itself when you sign in and search for your own business name.
realVsFake.fake: Your profile looks normal when you check it directly. Only the email claims anything is pending.

realVsFake.real: Google verifies a business through the profile's own dashboard, using a postcard, phone call, email or video.
realVsFake.fake: Verification is offered only through the emailed link, with a countdown and a form asking for the account password.

steps.title: Someone shared a document
steps.detail: An email in Google's sharing layout says a named person invited you to view 'Invoice_Q2_Final'. The blue 'Open' button and the small file icon look just as they should.

steps.title: Choose an account
steps.detail: Clicking Open shows a Google account picker, sometimes the genuine one. You select your address as you have done a hundred times before.

steps.title: The permission screen
steps.detail: Then a consent box appears: an app with a name like 'Docs' or 'Drive Viewer' wants to read, send and delete your email and see your contacts. One button says Allow.

steps.title: Access without a password
steps.detail: Pressing Allow gives the app a token that keeps working after you change your password. It reads your mail and forwards the same share invite to everyone in your address book.

google-docs-sharing-scam.whyItWorks: Shared documents are how offices run, and the account picker in the middle is often the real Google page, so every familiar check passes. The dangerous moment is a permissions box most people have learned to click through.

realVsFake.real: A document shared through Google opens directly if you are already signed in. Viewing it never requires granting an app access to your mail.
realVsFake.fake: An app you have never installed asks for permission to read and send email before any document appears.

realVsFake.real: Genuine shares also appear under 'Shared with me' in Drive, which you can check without touching the email.
realVsFake.fake: Nothing by that name is listed in 'Shared with me'. The file is just a button in the message.

realVsFake.real: A colleague sharing an invoice usually adds a note about what it is, and it relates to work you know about.
realVsFake.fake: The file name is generic, the note field is empty, and the sharer is someone you have had no dealings with.

steps.title: A sign-in you did not make
steps.detail: What arrives is a copy of Google's alert card: 'New sign-in on Windows', a city you have never visited, and two buttons, 'Yes, it was me' and 'No, secure account'.

steps.title: Securing the account
steps.detail: 'No, secure account' opens a page that looks like Google's sign-in. It asks you to 'confirm it's you' by typing your current password before you can change it.

steps.title: The relay
steps.detail: Software behind the page enters your password on the real Google site at the same moment. Google then sends a genuine code to your phone, or a tap-to-approve prompt.

steps.title: Code typed, account gone
steps.detail: The fake page asks for that code. Once you enter it or tap Yes, the criminal is signed in, replaces the recovery phone and email, and signs out your devices.

google-security-alert-scam.whyItWorks: Google does send sign-in alerts, and the correct response to a real one is to act quickly. The scam copies the one email you have been taught to take seriously, then uses your wish to protect the account as the way in.

realVsFake.real: Real alerts are also listed under Security in your Google Account, in the recent security activity panel.
realVsFake.fake: The supposed sign-in from a strange city is missing from your account's security activity. Only the email mentions it.

realVsFake.real: The safest route is Google's own Security Checkup, opened by typing the account address or through your phone's settings.
realVsFake.fake: The email says the account can be secured only through its button, and that the alert will expire.

realVsFake.real: A verification code arrives because someone is signing in at that moment. Google never needs it read back to 'cancel' anything.
realVsFake.fake: The page says entering the code will block the intruder, when in fact it completes the intruder's sign-in.

steps.title: A notice from 'HR'
steps.detail: Mid-morning, a message lands with a subject like 'Updated benefits: acknowledgement required by Friday'. The display name is 'Human Resources', but the address behind it is outside the company.

steps.title: The staff portal, copied
steps.detail: The link opens a page with your employer's logo, lifted from the public website, and the same single sign-on box you use for payslips and holiday requests.

steps.title: Username, password, approval
steps.detail: You enter your work login. If your company uses an authenticator prompt, the page waits while the criminal triggers a real one and you tap Approve.

steps.title: Payday goes elsewhere
steps.detail: Inside the real portal, the criminal changes the bank account your salary is paid into. Nothing looks wrong until payday, when the money lands in an account you have never seen.

hr-portal-email-scam.whyItWorks: Staff are used to HR emails that demand a click by a set date, and ignoring them usually earns a reminder from a manager. Benefits and payslips also concern your own money, so the message feels personal and worth opening.

realVsFake.real: HR announcements normally come from an internal address and are echoed on the intranet or by your manager.
realVsFake.fake: The sender is external, nobody else mentions the update, and your email system may tag it as coming from outside.

realVsFake.real: Most staff reach the portal from a bookmark or the intranet, where single sign-on logs them in without retyping anything.
realVsFake.fake: The emailed link asks for your full username and password from scratch, on an address that is not your company's.

realVsFake.real: A change to salary bank details usually triggers a confirmation from payroll, and many employers require a form or a call.
realVsFake.fake: The criminal changes the account quietly and filters the confirmation email out of your inbox so you never see it.

steps.title: Your storage is full
steps.detail: An email or text signed 'Apple' says your iCloud is full and that photos, documents and backups will be deleted in 48 hours. A bar graphic shows the storage maxed out in red.

steps.title: A cheap upgrade offer
steps.detail: The link opens a page offering 50 GB extra for a token sum, less than a coffee, as a 'loyalty reward'. A timer counts down beside a 'Claim upgrade' button.

steps.title: Sign in, then pay
steps.detail: You are asked for your Apple Account email and password, then a card number, expiry and security code to cover the small monthly fee.

steps.title: A much bigger charge
steps.detail: The token fee is never taken. The card is used for larger purchases or enrolled in a subscription under an unrelated company name, and the Apple login is tried on your real account.

icloud-storage-scam.whyItWorks: Many iPhone owners really are close to the free storage limit and have seen Apple's genuine 'storage almost full' banner. The threat is aimed at the one thing people cannot replace, years of photographs.

realVsFake.real: Apple does not delete existing photos because storage is full. New photos and backups simply stop uploading until you free space or upgrade.
realVsFake.fake: The message says everything already stored will be wiped in two days unless you pay now.

realVsFake.real: Storage is checked and upgraded in Settings, under your name and then iCloud, and billed to the payment method already on your account.
realVsFake.fake: The upgrade happens on a web page that asks you to type in a card from scratch.

realVsFake.real: Apple's storage plans have fixed, published prices. Surprise loyalty discounts do not arrive by text.
realVsFake.fake: A one-off bargain is offered to you alone, valid until a timer on the page reaches zero.

steps.title: Hype before anything exists
steps.detail: Paid influencer posts and a Telegram channel point to a slick site with a whitepaper, a countdown clock and a bar showing the presale almost filled.

steps.title: Whitelist forms and bonus tiers
steps.detail: You apply for the whitelist, then learn that bigger contributions earn bonus tokens. An admin messages privately to 'help you secure your allocation' before the round closes.

steps.title: Coins sent to the presale address
steps.detail: You send ETH, BNB or USDT to a wallet address shown on the page. A dashboard displays your token balance, though your own wallet holds nothing yet.

steps.title: A launch that keeps slipping
steps.detail: Listing day is postponed for an 'audit' or an 'exchange partnership'. Then the chat is muted, the site goes offline, or tokens arrive that no exchange will trade.

ico-presale-scam.whyItWorks: Everyone has heard about somebody who bought a coin for pennies before it listed, and a presale sells that exact seat. Because honest start-ups also raise money before the product exists, paying first seems normal.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate token sale names its founders, publishes a contract audit from a known firm and sets out vesting terms.
