realVsFake.fake: The team are cartoon avatars with first names, and the 'audit' is a badge image that links nowhere.

realVsFake.real: Established launchpads hold contributions in a contract with written refund rules if the raise fails.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to send coins straight to a personal wallet address pasted into a chat.

realVsFake.real: Serious projects warn that a new token can list below the sale price and stay there.
realVsFake.fake: Promoters name the multiple you will make on launch day and say the allocation closes within hours.

steps.title: A lawyer with your surname on file
steps.detail: An email from a 'barrister' abroad says his late client shared your surname, died without heirs and left a seven-figure estate. He proposes presenting you as next of kin.

steps.title: Paperwork covered in stamps
steps.detail: Reply, and he sends a death certificate, a 'certificate of deposit' and a bank letter. He asks for your passport copy, home address and bank details for the transfer.

steps.title: The first fee
steps.detail: Just before release, a cost appears: an affidavit, a probate stamp or an 'inheritance tax clearance' of a few hundred, payable by wire transfer to a named individual.

steps.title: Always one more charge
steps.detail: Once you pay, a new obstacle follows: an anti-money-laundering certificate, a courier bond, a bribe for an official. Each is larger, and each is described as the last.

inheritance-scam.whyItWorks: The email asks you to picture the money as already yours, so every fee looks tiny beside it. Once the first payment is sent, walking away means accepting that money is gone, which keeps people paying the next one.

realVsFake.real: Genuine heir-tracing firms identify you through family records and can explain exactly how you are related to the deceased.
realVsFake.fake: The only link is a shared surname, and the 'lawyer' openly suggests passing you off as a relative.

realVsFake.real: Genuine costs of administering an estate are paid out of the estate before the heirs receive their share.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to send fees from your own pocket, by wire or crypto, before a penny is released.

realVsFake.real: A real solicitor has a regulated firm, a listed office number and a professional email address you can look up independently.
realVsFake.fake: He writes from a free webmail account, gives only a mobile number, and insists the matter stay secret from your family.

steps.title: Your cover lapses tomorrow
steps.detail: Carrying your insurer's logo, the notice says your motor or home policy renews tomorrow, but the payment on file was declined. Without action you are uninsured from midnight.

steps.title: A renewal quote with a saving
steps.detail: The linked page shows a renewal price slightly below what you would expect, labelled an 'early payment saving', beside a 'Confirm and pay' button.

steps.title: Policyholder details
steps.detail: The form collects your name, date of birth, address, vehicle registration or property details and driving licence number, on the grounds that the policy must be 'matched'.

steps.title: A premium that buys nothing
steps.detail: You pay the premium by card. No policy is issued, the card is reused elsewhere, and you may be driving, or living in a home, with no cover and no idea.

insurance-email-scam.whyItWorks: Few people remember their exact renewal date, and driving uninsured carries real penalties, so 'lapses tomorrow' is hard to shrug off. Insurers also email constantly around renewal, which makes one more message from them unremarkable.

realVsFake.real: Insurers send renewal notices weeks ahead, quoting your policy number, the old premium and the new one.
realVsFake.fake: The notice arrives the day before, with no policy number or an invented one, and no comparison with last year.

realVsFake.real: If you pay by direct debit or stored card, renewal is normally collected automatically, and a failure is reported by letter or in your online account.
realVsFake.fake: You are told the only way to keep cover is to type card details into the linked page tonight.

realVsFake.real: After a real renewal you receive policy documents and, for a car, a certificate of insurance.
realVsFake.fake: After paying you get a generic 'thank you' page and nothing you could show anyone as proof of cover.

steps.title: Reading the mailbox first
steps.detail: Criminals break into a supplier's or customer's email account, or simply research who supplies whom, and note invoice formats, names and payment dates.

steps.title: The change-of-details letter
steps.detail: Shortly before a large invoice is due, accounts payable receives a polite email on the supplier's letterhead saying they have moved banks after an audit.

steps.title: A thread that looks continuous
steps.detail: The message sits inside a real email chain or comes from a domain one character off. A follow-up may ask you to confirm once records are updated.

steps.title: The scheduled payment run
steps.detail: The next payment leaves with the usual batch to the new account. Nobody notices until the real supplier chases an overdue invoice weeks later.

invoice-redirection-scam.whyItWorks: Suppliers do change banks, and updating a record is a routine clerical job that rarely gets a second look. The fraudulent email arrives in the middle of a real business relationship, quoting real invoice numbers, so it reads as ordinary admin.

realVsFake.real: A supplier changing bank is content for you to confirm by phoning the contact number you already hold.
realVsFake.fake: The email supplies a new phone number for 'verification', or says the usual contact is away.

realVsFake.real: Genuine new details normally stay in the supplier's own company name and home country.
realVsFake.fake: The replacement account is in a different name, at an online-only bank, or abroad.

realVsFake.real: Proper change requests go through a supplier onboarding form or portal, with sign-off from a second person.
realVsFake.fake: A single email with a PDF attachment asks for the amendment before Friday's payment run.

steps.title: A pitch about 'strategic land'
steps.detail: A sales agent phones, or you answer an advert, about plots on the edge of a growing town that are supposedly earmarked for new housing.

steps.title: The aerial photo and artist's impression
steps.detail: A glossy pack arrives showing a field divided into numbered plots, drawings of finished houses, and a 'planning consultant' predicting approval within two years.

steps.title: Reserving plot 47
steps.detail: A reservation fee holds your plot and the balance follows by bank transfer. You do receive a title document, because the field exists and your strip of it is registered.

steps.title: Planning consent never arrives
steps.detail: Years pass. The field is protected countryside or has no road access, the sales firm has dissolved, and no builder wants a patchwork of tiny plots with hundreds of owners.

land-banking-scam.whyItWorks: The title document is genuine and the field can be visited, which feels safer than shares. Buyers who have watched house prices climb nearby see a field beside a town as the same story at an earlier chapter.

realVsFake.real: Housebuilders acquire whole sites through land agents and option agreements after discussions with the planning authority.
realVsFake.fake: A sales office cuts one field into hundreds of garden-sized plots and sells them to the public by telephone.

realVsFake.real: The council's local plan and planning register are public, so anyone can see how a field is designated.
realVsFake.fake: The firm quotes its own consultant and discourages a call to the council, saying talks are 'at a confidential stage'.

realVsFake.real: A solicitor you choose checks access rights, restrictions on the title and what nearby farmland sells for.
realVsFake.fake: They supply a 'panel solicitor' and charge many times the agricultural value for each small strip.

steps.title: Cash in five minutes
steps.detail: An advert on social media or a text promotes an app lending small sums, with nothing needed except a selfie and an ID card.

steps.title: Handing over the phone book
steps.detail: Before any offer appears, the app requires permission for contacts, photos, location and SMS, and uploads the lot to its servers.

steps.title: A short loan with a slice missing
steps.detail: You request 100 and receive 65 after a 'service fee', with the full 100 plus interest due in seven days instead of the advertised three months.

steps.title: Shaming the borrower
steps.detail: On or before the due date, collectors message your family, colleagues and friends calling you a thief, and send edited obscene images made from your photos.

loan-app-scam.whyItWorks: People borrowing a small amount for an emergency tap 'Allow' on every permission box to reach the money. Nobody expects a lender to want their contact list, and by the time its purpose is clear the data is already copied.

realVsFake.real: A licensed lender states the total repayable, the interest rate and the term before you accept.
realVsFake.fake: The app shows one figure when you apply, then a shorter term and smaller payout after approval.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate lending apps check income and credit history, and have no use for your photo gallery or contacts.
realVsFake.fake: The loan cannot proceed until you grant access to everyone in your phone book.

realVsFake.real: A real lender chases arrears by letter, phone and formal notice, addressed to you alone.
realVsFake.fake: Collectors threaten to send your ID and doctored pictures to your employer and relatives within hours.

steps.title: An invoice from nobody in particular
steps.detail: Invoice INV-4821 is overdue and attached, the sender writes. It is short, businesslike and addressed to 'Accounts' or to no one, with a file named something like Invoice_4821.docm.

steps.title: A blurred page and a yellow bar
steps.detail: Opening the file shows a blurred document and a notice: 'This document is protected. Click Enable Editing, then Enable Content to view.' Word's yellow security bar sits above it.

steps.title: The click that runs the code
steps.detail: Enabling content runs a macro hidden in the file. It downloads a second program in the background, and the document either stays blurred or shows a bland invoice.

steps.title: Quiet collection
steps.detail: The installed program copies saved browser passwords and session cookies, watches for banking logins, and in an office can clear the way for ransomware across the network.

malware-attachment-scam.whyItWorks: People who handle invoices, CVs or delivery notes open attachments from strangers as part of the job, so refusing feels like not doing it. The yellow warning bar looks like a routine nuisance, and the document itself tells you to dismiss it.

realVsFake.real: A supplier's invoice is usually a plain PDF that displays straight away and names a purchase order or contact you recognise.
realVsFake.fake: The file is a macro-enabled document, a zip or an HTML page, and shows nothing readable until you click a button.

realVsFake.real: Ordinary documents never need macros switched on to be read. Macros automate spreadsheets. They are not needed to display text.
realVsFake.fake: The page claims it was 'created in an earlier version of Office' and can only be viewed once content is enabled.

realVsFake.real: A business chasing payment will have contacted you before and can be reached on a number from earlier dealings.
realVsFake.fake: The email is the first you have heard from them, and the phone number in the signature goes nowhere.

steps.title: A rep arrives with a savings sheet
steps.detail: A salesperson visits the shop or phones, glances at one card statement and announces they can cut your processing costs by a large margin.

steps.title: The headline rate
steps.detail: They quote one low debit rate and call the terminal 'free'. Monthly minimums, compliance charges and higher rates for credit and business cards go unmentioned.

steps.title: Two signatures on a tablet
steps.detail: You sign on a tablet at the counter. One signature is for processing, the other a separate equipment lease with a finance company, often for four or five years.

steps.title: Statements that don't match the pitch
steps.detail: Fees appear that were never discussed. Cancelling the processing leaves the lease running, and ending that means paying every remaining month at once.

merchant-services-scam.whyItWorks: Card statements are hard to read, so an owner cannot easily tell what they pay now, let alone test a rep's comparison. A promise of lower fees from someone standing at the counter during trading hours gets a signature before the paperwork gets read.

realVsFake.real: A fair provider gives a full written schedule of every rate and monthly charge, and leaves it with you to compare.
realVsFake.fake: The rep shows a one-page savings estimate, keeps the contract on their own tablet and wants it signed before they leave.

realVsFake.real: Card readers can be bought outright for a modest one-off price or rented on a short rolling term.
realVsFake.fake: A basic terminal is leased for years at a total many times its shop price, under a contract that cannot be cancelled.

realVsFake.real: Reputable processors state the exit terms plainly, and the same company handles both the reader and the processing.
realVsFake.fake: The seller is an independent agent, and complaints bounce between the processor, the leasing firm and a rep who has moved on.

steps.title: Your account number is already known
steps.detail: A fraudster holding your sort code and account number, from a cheque, an invoice or a leak, adds your account as a funding source on a payment app or brokerage.

steps.title: Two tiny credits appear
steps.detail: That service sends two deposits of a few pence or cents to prove ownership. You see odd small credits with a reference you do not recognise.

steps.title: A message asks for the amounts
steps.detail: A text, email or caller posing as your bank or the service says the deposits were a 'security test' and asks you to confirm both figures.

steps.title: The link goes live
steps.detail: Once the amounts are entered, the service treats the account as theirs to use and pulls money out by bank debit, in sums that grow.

micro-deposit-scam.whyItWorks: Receiving money feels harmless, and two amounts of a few pennies do not seem like a secret worth protecting. Hardly anyone realises that those figures work as a password proving control of the account.

realVsFake.real: Micro-deposits appear only after you have added your bank account to a service yourself, and you type the amounts into that service.
realVsFake.fake: The credits arrive when you have signed up for nothing, and a stranger wants the figures.

realVsFake.real: A company running the check never rings to ask what it sent, since it already knows.
realVsFake.fake: A caller says they need you to read out both amounts to 'cancel' or 'verify' the link.

realVsFake.real: Your bank can tell you which company sent a credit and can block future debits from it.
realVsFake.fake: The message warns you not to contact the bank because the 'test' will fail.

steps.title: Unusual sign-in activity
steps.detail: Microsoft's plain layout is copied closely: 'Sign-in details', a country, an IP address, a browser. Below, the fake adds something the real one never says: your account closes in 24 hours.

steps.title: The 'Review recent activity' button
steps.detail: The blue button opens a page with the four-colour logo and the 'Enter password' box used by Outlook and Hotmail. Your email address is already filled in.

steps.title: Password, then 'incorrect'
steps.detail: You type the password and the page says it was wrong, so you type it again. Both attempts are saved, then you are bounced to the genuine Microsoft site.

steps.title: The mailbox opens every other door
steps.detail: The criminal signs in to your Outlook, creates a rule hiding security emails, then uses 'forgot password' on shopping, banking and social accounts tied to that address.

microsoft-account-email-scam.whyItWorks: An old Hotmail or Outlook address is often the recovery email for everything else, so a threat to close it is alarming. The technical details, an IP address and a country, give the message an air of forensic accuracy.

realVsFake.real: A real unusual sign-in is listed on the Recent activity page of your Microsoft account, with the same time and location.
realVsFake.fake: Recent activity shows only your own sign-ins. The foreign login described in the email is nowhere to be found.

realVsFake.real: Microsoft closes accounts after long inactivity or at the owner's request. Missing a verification email is not a reason.
realVsFake.fake: The message threatens closure within a day unless you 'verify', a deadline with no basis in how accounts work.

realVsFake.real: The real sign-in page accepts a correct password the first time.
realVsFake.fake: The page rejects your password once whatever you type, so that it captures the same entry twice.

steps.title: A card on the doormat
steps.detail: A printed 'Sorry we missed you' card comes through the letterbox, often along a whole street, carrying a generic parcel logo instead of a known courier's name.

steps.title: Blank boxes where details belong
steps.detail: The spaces for sender, tracking number and time of visit are empty or scribbled. The only instruction is to phone a number or scan a QR code.

steps.title: A long wait on hold
steps.detail: The number is premium rate. Recorded messages, menu options and hold music keep you on the line while the per-minute charge builds on your phone bill.

steps.title: The redelivery website
steps.detail: Scanning the code opens a page that charges a rebooking fee by card and collects your address, for a parcel that was never on any van.

missed-delivery-card-scam.whyItWorks: A piece of card on the mat suggests that somebody physically came to the house, which feels more official than a text. People expect fraud on a screen, so paper gets less scrutiny.

realVsFake.real: A courier's card names the company, gives a reference number and says where the parcel is now, such as a neighbour or depot.
realVsFake.fake: The card says 'Parcel Delivery Service', quotes no reference and never mentions where the item is waiting.

realVsFake.real: Genuine couriers rearrange delivery through a free website or a standard-rate helpline.
realVsFake.fake: The contact number begins with a premium prefix such as 09 and is billed by the minute.

realVsFake.real: The real card usually has handwriting or a printed label added by the driver at your door.
realVsFake.fake: Every house on the road receives the identical pre-printed card on the same morning.

steps.title: The side-hustle offer
steps.detail: On social media or a student group, someone offers quick money to anyone with a bank account and a phone, calling it 'payment processing' or a 'flip'.

steps.title: Photos of cheques arrive
steps.detail: They send images of cheques made out to you, or ask for your banking login so they can deposit them through the app themselves.

steps.title: The balance jumps
steps.detail: The deposits show as available within a day. You are told to keep a couple of hundred and move the remainder by payment app, crypto or cash withdrawal.

steps.title: The account is closed
steps.detail: The cheques come back as counterfeit or stolen. The bank removes the money, pursues you for the shortfall, and may shut the account and report you.

mobile-deposit-scam.whyItWorks: Snapping a photo in a banking app hardly feels like handling a cheque at all, and the recruiter presents it as a harmless loophole. Young people short of cash see money appear overnight and take that as confirmation it is real.

realVsFake.real: Cheques you deposit by phone should be made out to you, for something you sold or were owed.
realVsFake.fake: The cheques come from a business you have never dealt with, sent as photos by a stranger.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate employer pays you through payroll and has no need to use your personal account.
realVsFake.fake: The 'job' consists only of receiving deposits and passing most of the money on.

realVsFake.real: Nobody with an honest reason asks for your online banking username and password.
realVsFake.fake: The recruiter says it is quicker if they log in as you and make the deposits themselves.

steps.title: A buyer who prefers paper
steps.detail: Someone answers your listing, agrees the price without haggling, and says they will post a money order because they are travelling or buying for a relative.

steps.title: The envelope holds too much
steps.detail: The money order arrives made out for 1,200 against an 800 item. A note explains the surplus covers the courier, and asks you to pass 400 on to their agent.

steps.title: Your bank shows the deposit
steps.detail: You pay it in at the counter and the balance goes up within a day or two. That is the bank advancing the funds, not confirming the paper is genuine.

steps.title: Counterfeit found, debit follows
steps.detail: Weeks later the issuer rejects the money order as a forgery. Your bank takes the full amount back, and the goods plus the 400 you forwarded are gone.

money-order-scam.whyItWorks: A money order feels like cash because someone supposedly paid for it up front at a post office or shop counter. When the bank credits it, sellers assume it has been checked, but the check against the issuer comes much later.

realVsFake.real: A genuine buyer sends a money order for the exact price and is happy for you to wait until the issuer confirms it.
realVsFake.fake: The amount is hundreds over, and the buyer wants the item posted and the change wired before you can check anything.

realVsFake.real: Money order issuers let you verify the serial number and amount with them directly before you release anything.
realVsFake.fake: The forgery has blurred print, a missing watermark or an amount that looks altered, and the buyer says there is no time to ring the issuer.

realVsFake.real: Someone who overpays by accident asks for the money order back so they can send a correct one.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to keep the paper and send the difference to a third person described as a shipper or agent.

steps.title: Good news with a catch
steps.detail: A message or call says a prize, parcel or approved loan is waiting, and only a small release fee stands between you and it.

steps.title: Only one way to pay
steps.detail: Card and bank transfer are refused with an excuse about tax or processing delays. You are sent to a Western Union or MoneyGram counter instead.

steps.title: A stranger's name on the form
steps.detail: The receiver is a private individual, often in another city or country, described as the company's cashier or agent. You may be coached on what to tell the clerk.

steps.title: The reference number is the key
steps.detail: Once you text over the tracking number from your receipt, the cash is collected within minutes using fake identification. A second fee is then invented.

money-transfer-service-scam.whyItWorks: Walking into a branded transfer counter feels official, and staff accept the cash without question. People assume a payment that needs a form and a receipt can be traced or cancelled later, when in practice a collected cash transfer is finished.

realVsFake.real: Transfer services are built for sending money to relatives and friends you know in person, and they say so on their forms.
realVsFake.fake: A business, lottery or lender asks you to wire a fee to a named individual you have never met.

realVsFake.real: The tracking number on your receipt is for you and the person collecting, nobody else.
realVsFake.fake: The caller stays on the line until you photograph the receipt and send it, then stops answering.

realVsFake.real: A real lender takes its charges out of the loan, and a real courier bills customs through its own checkout.
realVsFake.fake: Every fee must travel as cash to a different receiver name each time, and you are told to say it is a gift for family.

steps.title: An advert that ignores your credit
steps.detail: A social media ad or cold message promises mortgage approval whatever your credit file says, at a rate well below anything high street lenders quote.

steps.title: Approval in a single phone call
steps.detail: The 'broker' takes your income and address, asks for no payslips or bank statements, and rings back the same day to say a lender has agreed in principle.

steps.title: The rate lock fee
steps.detail: To hold the rate you must pay a 500 arrangement fee by bank transfer today. It is described as fully refundable when the mortgage completes.

steps.title: Insurance, valuation, then silence
steps.detail: More charges follow for a valuation or indemnity insurance. No offer letter from a lender ever arrives, and the phone number and website go dead.

mortgage-broker-scam.whyItWorks: People who have been turned down elsewhere badly want to hear yes, and real mortgages do involve arrangement and valuation fees. A refundable charge sounds like a small price for a rate that might vanish tomorrow.

realVsFake.real: A real broker appears on the financial regulator's public register under the same firm name and phone number they gave you.
realVsFake.fake: The firm name is close to a known lender's, but the register entry is missing or lists different contact details.

realVsFake.real: Lenders check payslips, bank statements and your credit file before saying yes, and some applicants are declined.
realVsFake.fake: Approval is guaranteed before anyone has seen a document, with the fee request arriving in the same call.

realVsFake.real: Genuine fees are itemised in a written mortgage illustration, and many can be added to the loan or paid at completion.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to transfer the fee to a personal account, with nothing in writing beyond a chat message promising a refund.

steps.title: A stealth drop is announced
steps.detail: A post in the project's Discord, often from a hijacked moderator account, or a reply under its X posts, says a surprise mint is live for fifteen minutes.

steps.title: The cloned mint page
steps.detail: The link opens a copy of the collection's site with the same artwork and a counter ticking down '312 left', hosted on a domain with one extra letter.

steps.title: Connect wallet, press Mint
steps.detail: Your wallet shows a request. Instead of a mint it is 'Set approval for all' or an unreadable signature that gives another address control of tokens you already hold.

steps.title: Drained in seconds
steps.detail: A script uses that permission to move your most valuable NFTs and tokens out at once. No new NFT arrives, and the announcement is deleted soon after.

nft-mint-scam.whyItWorks: Real collections do sell out in minutes, so collectors have learned that hesitating means missing the mint. A wallet pop-up looks much the same for a harmless mint and a drain, and speed beats reading.

realVsFake.real: Genuine projects announce mint dates days ahead on their verified accounts and repeat the contract address in several places.
realVsFake.fake: The mint is a 'surprise', announced once, in a DM or a channel locked so nobody can question it.

realVsFake.real: A true mint transaction calls a mint function and costs the stated price plus gas.
realVsFake.fake: The pop-up asks for blanket approval over your collections, which hands over what you already own.

realVsFake.real: Project moderators do not open private chats with members to hand out mint links.
realVsFake.fake: A 'mod' messages you first, says you made the whitelist and gives you ten minutes to claim.

steps.title: A refund or loan check appears
steps.detail: A text, advert or caller offers a tax refund, a loan eligibility check or a free budgeting tool, and says the quickest route is to connect your bank.

steps.title: Pick your bank from a list
steps.detail: The page shows a grid of bank logos, just as real open banking services do. Tapping yours hands you over to your own banking app to log in.

steps.title: The consent screen nobody reads
steps.detail: Your bank displays what is being granted: balances and past transactions, or a single payment to a named payee. People press 'Allow' expecting money to arrive.

steps.title: Consent becomes a withdrawal
steps.detail: The approval turns out to be a payment out of your account, or a data feed showing balances and salary dates that is used for a targeted follow-up call.

open-banking-scam.whyItWorks: The login happens inside your genuine banking app, with your real fingerprint or face check, so nothing looks fake. Because you never typed a password into a strange site, approving feels safe, and the wording on the consent screen goes unread.

realVsFake.real: Regulated open banking providers are listed on the financial regulator's register, and your bank names them on the consent screen.
realVsFake.fake: The name on the consent screen is one you have never heard of and does not match the app that sent you there.

realVsFake.real: Receiving a refund needs only your sort code and account number, or the original card. No connection to your bank is required.
realVsFake.fake: You are told money can only be paid in after you link your account and approve a prompt in your banking app.

realVsFake.real: A budgeting app asks for read-only access and explains how to switch it off in your bank's connected services menu.
realVsFake.fake: The request includes permission to make payments, which a refund or eligibility check has no use for.

steps.title: Sold at the asking price
steps.detail: A buyer, new client or remote employer agrees terms quickly and says their assistant or accounts department will handle the payment.

steps.title: An apology for sending extra
steps.detail: A cheque, card payment or transfer screenshot arrives showing 1,200 for a 900 sale. Minutes later comes an embarrassed message blaming a typing error.

steps.title: Send the 300 back today
steps.detail: They ask you to keep what you are owed and return the surplus straight away, to a different account from the one that paid, or as gift cards.

steps.title: The original payment unwinds
steps.detail: The cheque bounces, the stolen card is charged back, or the 'pending' transfer never lands. Your refund was real money and stays with them.

overpayment-scam.whyItWorks: Returning money that is not yours feels like plain honesty, and the buyer's apology makes refusing seem rude. The scam depends on the gap between a payment appearing in your account and that payment being final.

realVsFake.real: A person who pays too much by mistake asks their own bank or the payment app to reverse the original transaction.
realVsFake.fake: The 'buyer' wants a fresh payment from you, sent somewhere other than where the money came from.

realVsFake.real: An honest customer will wait the days it takes for a cheque to clear fully before expecting anything back.
realVsFake.fake: You hear about a flight, a sick child or an angry boss, all reasons the 300 cannot wait until tomorrow.

realVsFake.real: Real payment confirmations show in your own banking app or account history, where you can see whether funds are available.
realVsFake.fake: Proof arrives as a screenshot or a forwarded email with a payment company's logo, sent by the buyer themselves.

steps.title: A buyer takes your advert
steps.detail: You list coins on an exchange's P2P board. A buyer with a newly created account opens an order and starts messaging you in the trade chat straight away.

steps.title: A receipt picture arrives
steps.detail: They mark the order as paid and send an image of a banking app showing the transfer 'completed', sometimes with a forged email saying the exchange is holding your funds.

steps.title: Pressure in the chat
steps.detail: Your bank balance has not changed. They say transfers take hours, that another seller is waiting, and that they will open a dispute and wreck your rating.

steps.title: Release, and the coins go
steps.detail: You tap release and escrow hands the crypto over for good. The money never lands, or it comes from a stolen account and your bank later takes it back.

p2p-crypto-trade-scam.whyItWorks: In a P2P sale the release button is the seller's only brake. A receipt image looks like evidence, bank delays do happen, and nobody wants a dispute on their trading record, so releasing early feels like fairness.

realVsFake.real: An honest buyer pays from a bank account in the same name as their verified exchange profile, then waits while you check.
realVsFake.fake: Money comes from a different name, or exists only as an image, alongside pleas to release immediately.

realVsFake.real: Exchange staff speak only inside the official dispute screen, and escrow keeps the coins locked until you confirm receipt.
realVsFake.fake: A 'support agent' turns up on Telegram or by email telling you payment is verified and to release.

realVsFake.real: A genuine seller is content for coins to sit in escrow before you pay a penny.
realVsFake.fake: A fake seller offers a better rate if you pay him directly off the platform, then stops answering.

steps.title: Bad news with a payout
steps.detail: A message says your parcel was damaged at a sorting hub and that, as the recipient, you are owed 80 in compensation.

steps.title: A claim portal, already filled in
steps.detail: The link opens a claims page with a claim number pre-entered. It asks for your name, address and date of birth to 'match the policy'.

steps.title: Where to send the money
steps.detail: Next come sort code and account number, then card details 'to verify the account', and in some versions your online banking username and password.

steps.title: The claims team calls
steps.detail: Days later a caller who knows all of it says the payout needs a code approving. That code authorises a payment leaving your account.

parcel-insurance-claim-scam.whyItWorks: Being owed money lowers the guard that a demand for money raises. Supplying bank details to receive a payment seems logical, since that is how anyone gets paid, and the sum is modest enough to believe.

realVsFake.real: Compensation for a damaged parcel is claimed by the sender, or by you through the retailer after reporting the problem.
realVsFake.fake: The offer arrives before you knew anything was wrong, for an item it cannot name.

realVsFake.real: A genuine refund returns to the payment method used for the order, or the shop sends a replacement.
realVsFake.fake: The page wants a security code and banking password in order to pay you.

realVsFake.real: Real claims ask for evidence: photographs of the damage, the order number and the item's value.
realVsFake.fake: The form asks nothing about the goods and everything about your identity and accounts.

steps.title: A parcel waiting in a locker
steps.detail: A text says an item has been placed in a locker near you and will be removed in three days if not collected.

steps.title: Identify yourself for the code
steps.detail: Instead of showing a pickup code, the link asks for your name, mobile number, email and a card 'for identification' before it will reveal one.

steps.title: A request for your real code
steps.detail: If you do have something waiting, a follow-up message or call from the 'locker team' asks you to reply with the pickup code to confirm collection.

steps.title: Someone else opens the door
steps.detail: The code is all the machine checks. Whoever types it walks off with your parcel, the system logs a normal pickup, and the card from the form is abused separately.

parcel-locker-scam.whyItWorks: A locker code works like a key that anyone can use, with no signature and no handover in person. People think of it as a notification, so reading it out to 'the courier' seems harmless.

realVsFake.real: The locker operator sends the pickup code or QR automatically, together with the locker's street location.
realVsFake.fake: The text withholds the code until you complete a web form about yourself.

realVsFake.real: Courier staff have their own access to the compartments and never need the customer's code.
realVsFake.fake: A caller or texter asks you to read the digits out or forward the QR image.

realVsFake.real: A genuine notice names the retailer and which locker bank holds the item.
realVsFake.fake: It says only 'a locker near you' and gives no address, shop name or compartment number.

steps.title: New test results are ready
steps.detail: Results have been posted to your patient portal, the email announces, naming no clinic, doctor or test. Sometimes it is a statement instead: 'You have a balance due of 84.20.'

steps.title: A portal with a familiar look
steps.detail: The link opens a login page imitating a common portal system, with a stock photo of a nurse and boxes for username, password and date of birth.

steps.title: Verify your identity to continue
steps.detail: After logging in, a 'verification' form asks for your national insurance or Social Security number, insurer and member ID, and a card to settle the outstanding balance.

steps.title: Sold as a medical identity
steps.detail: No results ever appear. The details are bundled and used to bill insurers for treatment you never had, to order prescriptions, or to open credit in your name.

patient-portal-email-scam.whyItWorks: Anyone waiting on a biopsy, a scan or a blood test will open this email at once, and worry about the answer crowds out any thought about the sender. Real portals also send deliberately vague notices, for privacy reasons.

realVsFake.real: A real notice comes from the clinic or hospital you actually attended, after a test you remember having.
realVsFake.fake: The email names no provider, or one you have never visited, and you have had no tests recently.

realVsFake.real: You reach the genuine portal through the address on your appointment letter or the provider's app, with a login you set up yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The emailed link asks you to 'create or confirm' your login by supplying identity numbers the portal would already hold.

realVsFake.real: Medical bills arrive as itemised statements showing the date of service and what insurance has already paid.
realVsFake.fake: A round 'balance due' appears with no date or description, payable only through the card box on that page.

steps.title: A receipt for 499.99
steps.detail: A receipt arrives for a payment to a merchant you have never heard of, perhaps an antivirus firm or a crypto exchange, complete with a long transaction ID and today's date.

steps.title: 'Not you? Cancel here'
steps.detail: A line at the bottom says the purchase can be reversed within 24 hours, with a 'Dispute transaction' link and a helpline number for the 'billing desk'.

steps.title: The dispute form
steps.detail: The link opens a form asking for the card 'that was charged': the long number, expiry, security code, plus your online banking username 'so the refund can be matched'.

steps.title: A real charge follows the fake one
steps.detail: On the phone version, an agent says he must send a code to verify you. It is your bank's approval code for a payment he is making with your card as you speak.

payment-confirmation-email-scam.whyItWorks: The email never says which card was charged, so you cannot rule it out by glancing at one account. Disputing a payment feels like exercising a consumer right, and the form asks for what a dispute form would plausibly need.

realVsFake.real: A real charge appears in your banking app, usually as a pending transaction within minutes of the purchase.
realVsFake.fake: No pending payment of that amount shows on any card you own, however firmly the email insists.

realVsFake.real: You dispute a card payment with your own bank, using the number printed on the back of the card.
realVsFake.fake: The receipt tells you to dispute it with the 'merchant's billing desk', using contact details supplied in the same email.

realVsFake.real: A merchant refunding you already has the card on record and needs nothing more than the order reference.
realVsFake.fake: The form asks for the full card number and security code afresh, which is everything needed to spend on it.

steps.title: A refund is promised
steps.detail: Someone claiming to be a marketplace buyer, a utility agent or an old flatmate says they owe you money and will send it through your banking or payment app.

steps.title: A notification lands on your phone
steps.detail: The alert carries a friendly note such as 'Refund 85, tap to accept'. The note is free text written by the requester, not by the app.

steps.title: Approve to receive, they say
steps.detail: On the phone or in chat they talk you past the small print, where the button actually reads 'Pay' or 'Approve request' with your account as the source.

steps.title: Your PIN completes their request
steps.detail: You confirm with a PIN or fingerprint and 85 leaves your balance. When you query it, they send a second request to 'correct the error'.

payment-request-scam.whyItWorks: Request and payment screens look almost alike, and the scammer controls the one line of text people actually read. Anyone expecting money sees the word refund and a familiar app, then taps through from habit.

realVsFake.real: Incoming money needs nothing from you. It appears in your balance without a PIN, a tap or an approval.
realVsFake.fake: You are told the refund is 'waiting' and will expire unless you authorise it within a few minutes.

realVsFake.real: A genuine request-to-pay screen states the amount leaving your account and names who will receive it.
realVsFake.fake: The requester's display name is set to 'Refunds Dept' or a shop name, with the misleading instruction typed in the message field.

realVsFake.real: A shop refunding you sends the money to the card or account you originally paid from.
realVsFake.fake: The 'refund' comes through a person-to-person request from an individual profile created that week.

steps.title: A genuine email from PayPal
steps.detail: The criminal opens a PayPal business account, creates an invoice addressed to your email, and lets PayPal's own system send it. It passes spam filters and every sender check.

steps.title: The note from the 'seller'
steps.detail: The amount is 399.00 for an 'antivirus renewal' or 'Bitcoin purchase'. The seller's note field carries the real payload: 'If you did not authorise this, call our billing team', then a number.

steps.title: A fake PayPal agent
steps.detail: The person who answers says your account has been hacked, and that to block the charge you must install a 'security app', which is a remote-control tool, or confirm your login aloud.

steps.title: Paying to cancel
steps.detail: He directs you to send a 'reversal payment', buy gift cards, or log in to your bank while he watches. Others simply click 'Pay invoice' in a panic, which sends the money.

paypal-invoice-scam.whyItWorks: Every check people are taught passes: the sender is really PayPal, the links go to the real site, and the invoice shows in your account. The only false part is the phone number, typed into a free-text note that PayPal did not write.

realVsFake.real: An invoice is only a request. Nothing leaves your account unless you press Pay, and unwanted ones can be ignored or reported inside PayPal.
realVsFake.fake: The note claims the amount 'will be auto-debited within 24 hours' unless you ring to stop it.

realVsFake.real: PayPal's contact details are found in the Help section after you log in. They are never written in a seller's note.
realVsFake.fake: The only phone number offered sits inside the invoice text, supplied by the stranger who sent the bill.

realVsFake.real: PayPal staff do not ask you to install software, share your screen or move money to protect an account.
realVsFake.fake: Within minutes the 'agent' wants a remote-access app on your phone and your banking open in front of him.

steps.title: Staff names gathered from public profiles
steps.detail: The fraudster picks an employee from the company website or a professional networking profile, and notes who handles payroll and when staff are paid.

steps.title: A short note to HR
steps.detail: An email in the employee's name says they have switched banks and asks what is needed to update their direct deposit before the next pay run.

steps.title: The form comes back filled in
steps.detail: Payroll replies with a change form. It is returned within the hour carrying new routing and account numbers, often for a prepaid card or online-only bank.

steps.title: Payday goes to the wrong account
steps.detail: Salary is sent to the new account and withdrawn the same day. The loss surfaces only when the real employee asks where their wages are.

payroll-direct-deposit-scam.whyItWorks: Changing bank is an ordinary life event, and payroll teams process such requests every month without fuss. The email is brief, polite and names a real colleague, so nothing about it invites a second look near a busy payday.

realVsFake.real: Employees usually change their pay details themselves in the HR self-service portal, behind their own login.
realVsFake.fake: The sender says they are locked out of the portal or travelling, and asks payroll to key the change in for them.

realVsFake.real: A real colleague writes from their work address and will happily confirm on an internal call or at their desk.
realVsFake.fake: The display name is right but the address behind it is a free webmail account or a domain one letter off.

realVsFake.real: Genuine changes often come with a voided cheque or bank letter and can wait a pay cycle if needed.
realVsFake.fake: The request stresses that it must take effect this cycle and goes quiet when asked to ring the number on file.

steps.title: The free pension review
steps.detail: A cold call, text or web advert offers a no-cost review, claiming your old workplace pension is 'frozen' or performing badly in an outdated fund.

steps.title: Forms brought to your door
steps.detail: A smartly dressed consultant or a courier brings paperwork: a letter of authority to obtain your pension details and transfer forms, sometimes with talk of a loophole for early cash.

steps.title: The pot moves to a new scheme
steps.detail: Your savings transfer into an obscure scheme and from there into overseas hotel rooms, forestry or storage units. A cash 'bonus' may be paid to you as a sweetener.

steps.title: Statements stop coming
steps.detail: Intermediaries take large fees on the way through. Later the statements dry up, the investment cannot be sold, and the tax office may bill you for money released early.

pension-scam.whyItWorks: A pension is often the largest sum a person owns, yet few have looked at theirs in years or know how it is invested. A free check-up from someone who names your old employer sounds like help.

realVsFake.real: Regulated advisers appear on the financial regulator's register, and you can ring the firm on the number listed there.
realVsFake.fake: The firm says it 'only introduces' so needs no authorisation, or borrows the name of a genuine adviser.

realVsFake.real: Your existing provider lets a transfer take weeks, sends risk warnings and will answer questions before anything moves.
realVsFake.fake: A courier waits on the doorstep while you sign, because the offer 'closes on Friday'.

realVsFake.real: A proper adviser charges a stated fee and usually recommends mainstream, regulated funds you can sell.
realVsFake.fake: The review costs nothing, yet the return is guaranteed and comes from one unusual asset abroad.

steps.title: A tip from someone you trust
steps.detail: A friend, relative or fellow member of your church or club mentions a fund that has paid them on the same date every month without fail.

steps.title: The test deposit pays
steps.detail: You put in a little. Payments arrive on the exact day with a tidy statement, and the explanation is a trading bot or currency arbitrage nobody can describe.

steps.title: Roll it over, bring a friend
steps.detail: The promoter suggests leaving payouts in to compound and offers commission for each person you introduce. You add your savings and tell your family about it.

steps.title: Withdrawals hit a 'system upgrade'
steps.detail: When fresh deposits slow, cash-out requests meet an audit, a lock-in period or a platform migration. Then the dashboard and the promoter both go quiet.

ponzi-scheme-scam.whyItWorks: The first payouts are real money in your bank, introduced by a person you already trust. Having watched the scheme pay, people stop asking where the profit comes from and become its most convincing recruiters.

realVsFake.real: Genuine funds have bad months, and their statements show losses alongside gains with assets held by an independent custodian.
realVsFake.fake: The return is identical every month whatever markets do, and the method is a 'proprietary' secret.

realVsFake.real: A regulated fund appears on the regulator's register, issues audited accounts and takes money through a client account.
realVsFake.fake: Deposits go to a personal bank account or crypto wallet, and your balance exists only on their dashboard.

realVsFake.real: Investment firms do not pay clients a commission for signing up relatives.
realVsFake.fake: Referral bonuses and 'ranks' reward you for bringing in workmates, because new deposits fund old payouts.

steps.title: The hotel-ballroom seminar
steps.detail: A free evening seminar or social media advert promotes 'hands-off' units: student pods, hotel rooms or off-plan flats abroad, each with rent 'assured' for five years.

steps.title: Renderings and a yield table
steps.detail: You are shown computer-generated images, a table of projected income and a rental guarantee issued by a management company the developer quietly owns.

steps.title: Reserve tonight for the discount
steps.detail: A reservation fee paid on the night secures a 'launch price'. Within weeks, staged payments of half the price or more go directly to the developer's account.

steps.title: A hoarding and a hole
steps.detail: Progress photos show the same fenced site for months. The developer enters administration, and the promised rent turns out to have been backed by nothing.

property-investment-scam.whyItWorks: Bricks and mortar feel dependable, and a contract with assured rent removes the one worry a first-time landlord has. A seminar room where other buyers are reaching for reservation forms supplies the rest of the push.

realVsFake.real: An established developer has finished buildings you can visit, with planning consent and land ownership on public record.
realVsFake.fake: There are only renderings, and the site still belongs to someone else or lacks permission to build.

realVsFake.real: Stage payments normally sit with a solicitor or in a protected account until building milestones are certified.
realVsFake.fake: Money goes straight to the developer or an overseas sales agent, with a discount for paying more upfront.

realVsFake.real: Honest agents say rent depends on finding tenants, and suggest you use your own independent lawyer.
realVsFake.fake: The 'assured' rent is paid out of buyers' own deposits for a while, and the recommended lawyer works for the seller.

steps.title: Three messages on hold
steps.detail: Laid out like a system report, the message shows a small table of three held emails, with senders such as 'Accounts Payable' and subjects like 'Remittance advice', each beside a 'Release' link.

steps.title: Signed by your own domain
steps.detail: The notice is signed 'Mail Administrator' for your own email domain, inserted automatically from your address, and says the items will be purged in 24 hours.

steps.title: Release to inbox
steps.detail: Clicking Release opens a webmail login with your address pre-filled and your company's logo pulled in automatically. It asks for the password to 'authenticate the release'.

steps.title: No messages, one lost mailbox
steps.detail: The page reports 'messages released' or redirects to your real webmail. No held emails ever arrive, and the criminal now signs in to read your mail and reset other accounts.

quarantined-email-scam.whyItWorks: The held subject lines hint at money or a client waiting, so you want to see them. Spam filters do hold genuine mail by mistake, and most staff have no idea what their company's real quarantine notice looks like.

realVsFake.real: Real quarantine digests come from the filtering service your IT team set up, at the same time each day, listing mail you can recognise as spam.
realVsFake.fake: This one arrives once, without warning, and every held message sounds like something you would want.

realVsFake.real: Releasing a message from a real quarantine usually takes one click, or a visit to a portal where you are already signed in.
realVsFake.fake: The release link demands your mailbox password on a page hosted somewhere unrelated to your provider.

realVsFake.real: Personal accounts with Gmail or Outlook put suspect mail in a Spam or Junk folder. They do not email you about held messages.
realVsFake.fake: A 'security filter' claims to be holding mail for a free webmail address that has no quarantine at all.

steps.title: Reading a hacked inbox
steps.detail: Criminals get into the email account of a solicitor, estate agent or title company and quietly read the threads to learn who is buying what and when.

steps.title: Waiting for completion week
steps.detail: They hold back until the deposit or closing funds are about to be requested, so their message will land exactly when you expect bank details.

steps.title: The 'updated client account' email
steps.detail: A reply in the genuine thread, with the firm's signature and your property address, says the client account has changed and earlier instructions should be disregarded.

steps.title: House money sent abroad
steps.detail: You wire the funds and confirm by email. The money is split across other accounts within hours, and the real firm rings days later asking where it is.

real-estate-wire-fraud-scam.whyItWorks: The message quotes your real case reference, purchase price and completion date, taken from the hacked mailbox. Buyers are anxious about losing the house over a late payment, so an instruction marked time-sensitive gets obeyed without a phone call.

realVsFake.real: Conveyancers give client account details at the start, often on paper, and warn that they will not change them by email.
realVsFake.fake: New account details appear the day before completion, with a line telling you to ignore everything sent before.

realVsFake.real: The firm's account is held in the firm's name, at a bank in the country where the property is.
realVsFake.fake: The payee is an individual or an unrelated trading company, sometimes at a bank in another region entirely.

realVsFake.real: Staff welcome a call to their office switchboard to read the account number back before you send anything.
realVsFake.fake: The email says the office phones are down or the solicitor is in meetings, and offers a new mobile number instead.

steps.title: A recruiter finds your CV
steps.detail: Someone from an agency you have not heard of messages on a job board or chat app, saying your profile suits a role with good pay and an immediate start.

steps.title: A ten-minute interview
steps.detail: A short text chat or call covers little beyond your availability. The same day you are told you are a great fit and an offer letter is attached.

steps.title: Fees before a start date
steps.detail: Before the start date can be confirmed you must cover registration and a background check, payable to the agency by bank transfer or gift card.

steps.title: Training, uniform, then no reply
steps.detail: Further charges follow for a training course, a uniform or a work laptop. The start date keeps moving until the recruiter's profile disappears.

recruitment-fee-scam.whyItWorks: Background checks and training are normal parts of starting work, so the fees sound like routine onboarding. Someone who has been job hunting for months is told the post is already theirs, and paying feels like the last formality.

realVsFake.real: Recruitment agencies are paid by the employer who hires you. Finding you a job costs you nothing.
realVsFake.fake: The agency's income is the candidate, charged for registration, vetting and equipment before any work exists.

realVsFake.real: A real recruiter names the hiring company and arranges an interview with someone who works there.
realVsFake.fake: The employer is 'a confidential client', and every conversation stays with one person on a messaging app.

realVsFake.real: Where a criminal record check is needed, the employer arranges it through the official checking service.
realVsFake.fake: You are sent a link to a private payment page and told the check must be bought through the agency's own provider.

steps.title: A subscription refund call
steps.detail: A caller says an antivirus or streaming renewal was cancelled and you are due 500 back. They only need to guide you through the refund form.

steps.title: Screen sharing to 'help'
steps.detail: You are walked through installing a remote support tool such as AnyDesk, then asked to open online banking so the refund can be 'verified'.

steps.title: An extra zero on the form
steps.detail: They blank your screen, shift 5,000 from your savings into your current account, then show you the balance and cry out that they typed too much.

steps.title: Begging for 4,500 back
steps.detail: The caller pleads that they will be sacked, and asks you to return the difference by bank transfer, gift cards or cash in a parcel.

refund-recovery-scam.whyItWorks: You watch your own balance jump, so the overpayment looks proven. The money was yours all along, moved from another of your accounts, but the caller's panic about losing their job pushes you to fix their mistake before checking where it came from.

realVsFake.real: Companies refund the card that paid, automatically, and tell you by email. No call or software is involved.
realVsFake.fake: A refund agent phones you and says the money cannot be sent until you install a program.

realVsFake.real: If a business overpays you, its finance team recalls the payment through the bank. Staff do not phone to plead.
realVsFake.fake: The caller sobs about their children and their manager, then gets angry when you suggest ringing your bank first.

realVsFake.real: A true incoming credit shows a sender name in your statement, and your other accounts are untouched.
realVsFake.fake: The 'refund' has no outside sender, and your savings balance has dropped by exactly the same amount.

steps.title: Looking up how to return
steps.detail: You search for a shop's returns page and click a sponsored result, or an email arrives after a purchase inviting you to 'start your return'.

steps.title: A lookalike returns centre
steps.detail: The page copies the retailer's colours and asks for your order number, email and account password so it can 'locate the order'.

steps.title: Paying for the label
steps.detail: A return shipping fee of 4.95 is requested by card before a printable label will be generated, with a note that the return window closes soon.

steps.title: A label to nowhere
steps.detail: The PDF carries a barcode no drop-off shop can scan, or a private address. The parcel vanishes, no refund comes, and the card is charged again.

return-label-scam.whyItWorks: Returns are a chore with a deadline, and every shop handles them differently, so an unfamiliar portal does not stand out. Plenty of real retailers charge for postage back, which makes the fee look ordinary.

realVsFake.real: Genuine returns start from the order history in your account, which then issues a label or QR code.
realVsFake.fake: An advert or email leads to a standalone 'returns centre' that makes you sign in a second time.

realVsFake.real: Where a real shop charges for sending goods back, it usually deducts the cost from the refund.
realVsFake.fake: Card details are taken upfront on the page, before any label exists.

realVsFake.real: A real label shows the retailer's warehouse and a tracking number that works on the carrier's site.
realVsFake.fake: The label names an unrelated address, and the tracking reference returns no result anywhere.

steps.title: A token appears overnight
steps.detail: A new coin with a meme name launches on a decentralised exchange. Paid 'callers', X accounts and a busy Telegram post rocket emojis and a rising chart.

steps.title: Reassuring buzzwords
steps.detail: The pitch lists 'liquidity locked', 'contract renounced' and 'devs doxxed', perhaps with a face on video. The lock runs for days, or covers a sliver of the pool.

steps.title: The chart climbs
steps.detail: Buys from the team's own wallets push the price up. You swap ETH or SOL for the token and watch your holding multiply on screen.

steps.title: The pool is emptied
steps.detail: In one transaction the developers withdraw the pooled funds or dump a hidden supply. The price hits near zero within a minute, and some contracts block selling altogether.

rug-pull-scam.whyItWorks: The chart is the advert. A price that has already tripled looks like proof, and phrases such as 'liquidity locked' sound like safeguards to anyone who cannot read the contract code behind them.

realVsFake.real: Established tokens have a long trading history, thousands of holders and liquidity that no single wallet can remove.
realVsFake.fake: A handful of linked wallets hold most of the supply, and the deployer can withdraw the pool.

realVsFake.real: Teams with reputations at stake publish their code, pass outside audits and build something before selling.
realVsFake.fake: The product is a logo and a roadmap ending in 'moon', and the chat bans anyone asking about selling.

realVsFake.real: With a sound token, a small test sale goes through at roughly the quoted price.
realVsFake.fake: Test sales fail or lose most of their value to a hidden 'tax' written into the contract.

steps.title: The fraud team rings you
steps.detail: The call displays your bank's real number. A calm voice gives a name and staff ID, then asks whether you just tried to pay 900 to an electronics shop.

steps.title: Your account is 'under attack'
steps.detail: When you say no, they explain that criminals, possibly helped by branch staff, have access to your account and every pound in it is at risk.

steps.title: A new account, already opened
steps.detail: They read out a sort code and account number said to be freshly created in your name, and tell you to transfer your balance there.

steps.title: Coached past the bank's warnings
steps.detail: You are told to ignore the app's fraud warning and the name mismatch alert, and to say 'paying a friend' if asked. Savings follow in several transfers.

safe-account-scam.whyItWorks: The caller already knows your name, address and part of your card number, usually from an earlier phishing text, so they sound like the bank. Hearing that staff are involved explains in advance why you must not hang up and call the branch.

realVsFake.real: A bank that suspects fraud freezes the card or blocks the payment itself. Your money stays where it is.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to do the moving, by making a transfer from your own app to an account number read over the phone.

realVsFake.real: No bank or police force asks a customer to lie to branch staff or click past a fraud warning.
realVsFake.fake: The caller says the warnings are part of the attack and that telling anyone could tip off the insider.

realVsFake.real: Genuine fraud staff are content for you to hang up and ring the number printed on your card.
realVsFake.fake: They keep you on the line for an hour or more and warn that your money will be gone if the call drops.

steps.title: You ask for help in public
steps.detail: You post on X, Reddit or Discord that your wallet will not sync. Within minutes, replies arrive from accounts named after MetaMask, Trust Wallet or Ledger support.

steps.title: The 'wallet validation' tool
steps.detail: The agent sends a link to a rectification page showing logos for dozens of wallets. You pick yours and it pretends to connect, then reports an error.

steps.title: Type your twelve words
steps.detail: A 'manual import' box appears with numbered fields for the recovery phrase, twelve or twenty-four words, described as the only way to resync.

steps.title: Restored on a stranger's phone
steps.detail: The criminal enters the phrase into their own wallet app and sends everything out. No password, device or two-step check stands in the way, because the phrase is the wallet.

seed-phrase-phishing-scam.whyItWorks: Crypto has no phone line to ring, so a person with a stuck wallet takes help where it appears. The fake agent arrives at the peak of worry, and 'validating' sounds like upkeep, not handing over keys.

realVsFake.real: Wallet makers say their staff will never ask for a recovery phrase. It is typed only into the wallet app when restoring.
realVsFake.fake: A web form, chat agent or email asks for the phrase to 'sync', 'validate' or 'migrate' your wallet.

realVsFake.real: Official support is reached from inside the app or the maker's help centre and works through tickets.
realVsFake.fake: 'Support' finds you by direct message seconds after your post and wants to continue on Telegram.

realVsFake.real: Wallet upgrades arrive as ordinary app updates from the official store or the maker's site.
realVsFake.fake: A notice says your wallet must be moved to 'version two' by a deadline or the funds vanish.

steps.title: A recorded call about your listing
steps.detail: An automated voice or cold caller says your Google business listing is unverified or about to be marked closed, and asks you to press one.

steps.title: Borrowing Google's name
steps.detail: The agent introduces themselves as a 'Google specialist' or certified partner, and reads your address and opening hours back to you from the public listing.

steps.title: A guaranteed first-page package
steps.detail: They offer to fix the listing and put you top of search for a monthly fee, taken by card on the call under a twelve-month agreement.

steps.title: Junk links and a login handed over
steps.detail: The work is a batch of spam backlinks or nothing at all. Some ask for your listing login, then hold the profile hostage when you cancel.

seo-services-scam.whyItWorks: Most owners know their search listing brings in customers but not how ranking is decided, so a threat to remove it lands hard. A caller using Google's name and quoting the shop's own details sounds like the company that controls the listing.

realVsFake.real: A Google business listing is free to hold, and Google does not ring owners to sell ranking or threaten removal.
realVsFake.fake: The caller says a payment is needed today to keep the listing live or to 'renew verification'.

realVsFake.real: Honest search agencies explain that nobody can promise a position, and report on traffic and enquiries month by month.
realVsFake.fake: The pitch guarantees the number one spot within weeks, usually for a phrase nobody actually searches for.

realVsFake.real: A reputable agency works under your ownership of the listing and website, with access you can revoke.
realVsFake.fake: They ask for your password or to be made primary owner, which lets them lock you out of your own profile.

steps.title: You are a class member
steps.detail: You are told you are entitled to 740 from a settlement with a well-known company over a data breach or hidden fees. A 'claim ID' and a 'notice ID' are quoted.

steps.title: The claims website
steps.detail: A link opens a site with a court-style crest, a case caption and a claim form. It resembles a real settlement administrator's page and may copy text from an actual case.

steps.title: Choose how to be paid
steps.detail: The form asks for your full name, address, date of birth and Social Security or national insurance number, then bank account and routing number or sort code for 'direct deposit'.

steps.title: A fee before release
steps.detail: A final page asks for a small 'processing' or 'disbursement' fee by card before the 740 is released. The fee is taken, the card kept, and no payout arrives.

settlement-email-scam.whyItWorks: Real settlement notices do arrive by email out of the blue, from administrators nobody has heard of, about cases nobody remembers joining. A fake one is hard to tell apart, and a modest sum like 740 sounds more credible than a fortune.

realVsFake.real: Claiming from a real settlement is free. Legal fees and administration costs come out of the settlement fund by order of the court.
realVsFake.fake: You must pay a processing charge by card before your share can be 'disbursed'.

realVsFake.real: A real notice gives a case name and court you can look up, and a deadline that is typically months away.
realVsFake.fake: The case cannot be found in any court record or news report, and the claim window closes in days.

realVsFake.real: Administrators generally need a claim ID and a mailing address or payment choice, and rarely more identity detail than that.
realVsFake.fake: The form wants your full identity number and online banking details for a payment of a few hundred.

steps.title: Premium is about to end
steps.detail: A green-and-black email says Spotify could not collect your latest payment and Premium is on hold. Within 24 hours you will drop to the free tier, adverts and all.

steps.title: The 'Retry payment' button
steps.detail: The green button opens a login page on a lookalike address. Many people have used one Spotify password for years and share it with other sites, which is what the criminal wants.

steps.title: Card details for a tenner
steps.detail: A billing page then asks for card number, expiry, security code and the name on the card, to retry a charge of around ten pounds.

steps.title: Two things to sell
steps.detail: The card is tested with small purchases, then used or sold. The login is sold separately as a cheap 'Premium account', and tried against your email and shopping accounts.

spotify-payment-scam.whyItWorks: A music subscription renews so quietly that nobody remembers the billing date, which makes a failed payment entirely believable. Losing downloaded playlists before a commute or a gym session is a small, immediate irritation that invites a quick fix.

realVsFake.real: Spotify shows your plan, next billing date and payment method on your account page, reachable from the app's settings.
realVsFake.fake: The email hides those details and gives only a button, with no mention of when the payment was attempted.

realVsFake.real: If a real payment fails, the account quietly reverts to the free version. Your playlists and saved music stay where they are.
realVsFake.fake: The message warns that your library, playlists and followers will be permanently removed if you miss the deadline.

realVsFake.real: Updating a card on the real site happens after login, on one form, and never involves your banking password.
realVsFake.fake: The page asks for login and card together, and sometimes for a bank 'verification' password as a third step.

steps.title: A thank-you from a familiar brand
steps.detail: Borrowing the logo of a supermarket, pharmacy or parcel company, the message says you were picked to give feedback. Thirty seconds of questions earns a 90 reward.

steps.title: Five easy questions
steps.detail: The survey asks how often you shop and how you rate the staff. Whatever you answer, a spinning animation ends with 'Congratulations, you qualify'.

steps.title: Pick your prize
steps.detail: A page shows a tablet, headphones or gift card marked 'only 2 left', with invented comments underneath from happy winners. You choose one and are asked to cover 3.95 shipping.

steps.title: The small print
steps.detail: The card form sits above pale grey text enrolling you in a 'membership' billed every two weeks at a far higher amount, under a company name you will not recognise on the statement.

survey-reward-email-scam.whyItWorks: Answering the questions first makes the prize feel earned, so the shipping fee seems like a fair last step. A charge of 3.95 is small enough that people hand over a card number without reading what else it authorises.

realVsFake.real: Genuine brand surveys are linked from a till receipt or your account, and offer a prize-draw entry or a modest voucher.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger's email offers a 90 reward to everyone who clicks, for half a minute of multiple choice.

realVsFake.real: When a retailer gives a real reward, it is a code or points added to your loyalty account with nothing to pay.
realVsFake.fake: The 'free' gift needs a card payment for postage, taken by a company that is not the brand named in the email.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate subscription states its price beside the payment button and sends a confirmation with cancellation details.
realVsFake.fake: The recurring charge is disclosed only in faint text far down the page, and no confirmation email ever arrives.

steps.title: Your year-end form is ready
steps.detail: In the weeks before the filing deadline, an email says your W-2, P60 or annual tax statement is available. It appears to come from 'Payroll' or a tax document service.

steps.title: A file called TaxForm.html
steps.detail: Instead of a PDF, the attachment is a web page file. Opened, it loads in your browser from your own computer and displays a login box over a blurred tax form.

steps.title: Sign in to unblur
steps.detail: The box asks for your work email password or payroll login 'to decrypt the document'. In the link version, the download is a zip holding a program disguised with a PDF icon.

steps.title: Used before you file
steps.detail: A stolen payroll login exposes your real tax form, with identity number, salary and address, which is enough to file a false return and claim the refund in your name.

tax-document-email-scam.whyItWorks: Timing does most of the work: in tax season, employers and banks really do email to say forms are ready, and people are waiting for them. An .html attachment looks like a harmless document to anyone who does not check file endings.

realVsFake.real: Employers usually tell staff in advance when year-end forms will be issued and where, typically inside the payroll system.
realVsFake.fake: The email arrives with no prior announcement and puts the 'form' in an attachment or behind its own download link.

realVsFake.real: A real tax form is a PDF or a page inside your payroll account. Once open, it does not ask for a password.
realVsFake.fake: The attachment ends in .html, .zip or .iso and shows a login prompt on top of an unreadable form.

realVsFake.real: Payslips and year-end forms come from the same sender and system as every previous one.
realVsFake.fake: The display name says 'Payroll Department', but the address behind it is a domain you have never seen.

steps.title: A problem with your return
steps.detail: The sender poses as the tax-preparation service you filed with, or a popular one mailed to everyone. Your return was rejected, it says, or your refund is on hold pending verification.

steps.title: A clone of the software's login
steps.detail: The link opens a clone of the software's login page, down to the padlock artwork. You enter your user ID and password, then the code texted to your phone.

steps.title: 'Confirm your filing details'
steps.detail: A follow-up form asks for last year's income figure, your identity number, date of birth and the bank account for the refund, all 'to re-submit the return'.

steps.title: The refund is redirected
steps.detail: Signed in as you, the criminal downloads prior returns, files or amends this year's with his own bank details, and the tax refund is paid to him.

tax-software-email-scam.whyItWorks: People who file through software expect emails from it during tax season, including genuine rejection notices. A held refund is money you are already counting on, and the filing deadline makes any hitch feel like it must be fixed today.

realVsFake.real: A real rejection shows as a status when you open the software yourself, with the error code and the field to correct.
realVsFake.fake: The email gives no reason for the hold and no error code, only a button marked 'Verify account'.

realVsFake.real: Tax refunds are paid by the tax authority into the account named on your return. The software company does not hold them back.
realVsFake.fake: The message says the software firm itself is keeping your refund until you log in and re-verify.

realVsFake.real: Genuine services write to the address you registered and greet you by the name on the account.
realVsFake.fake: The same email reaches people who have never used that product, addressed to 'Dear taxpayer'.

steps.title: A teammate is trying to reach you
steps.detail: The email mimics a Teams activity notice: purple banner, a colleague's initials in a circle, the first words of a message, 'Hi, are you free for a quick...', and 'Reply in Teams'.

steps.title: A missed call from the boss
steps.detail: Other versions say a director tried to call you, or that you were added to a channel named after a real project. The names are scraped from the company website or LinkedIn.

steps.title: The work sign-in page
steps.detail: 'Reply in Teams' opens a Microsoft 365 login clone. It takes your work email and password, then relays the authenticator number or code and captures the session.

steps.title: Inside the company chat
steps.detail: Using your account, the criminal reads chats and shared files, then messages real colleagues from within Teams itself, where a link from you is trusted without question.

teams-notification-email-scam.whyItWorks: An unanswered message from a manager creates social pressure that an ordinary email does not. The truncated preview is designed so you cannot tell what is being asked without clicking, and replying fast feels like plain good manners.

realVsFake.real: A real Teams message is waiting in the app on your laptop or phone, with a red badge on the Chat icon.
realVsFake.fake: The app shows no unread chat and no missed call from that colleague. Only the email says otherwise.

realVsFake.real: Missed-activity emails are sent after you have been inactive in Teams for a while, and clicking normally opens the app you are already signed in to.
realVsFake.fake: The notice arrives while you are sitting in Teams, and its button asks for your password as if you were new.

realVsFake.real: Chat messages sit in the conversation history. They do not vanish because you were slow to read them.
realVsFake.fake: The email claims the two messages will 'expire' unless you sign in to read them today.

steps.title: Added to a group overnight
steps.detail: You find yourself in a Telegram or WhatsApp group of several hundred people, or an 'assistant' invites you after you click an advert using a famous investor's face.

steps.title: The professor and his helper
steps.detail: A mentor posts market commentary each morning while an assistant answers questions. Members share winning screenshots and thank the teacher, and most of those accounts are run by the organisers.

steps.title: Free signals, then the real ask
steps.detail: After a week of free tips, a coin is named with ten minutes' notice, or you are told to open an account on a 'partner platform' to copy trades.

steps.title: Profits you cannot withdraw
